Jesus said the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way so that whoever believes in Him will have eternal life. This foretells the cross. Just as the dying did not have to earn or even understand but only look, sinners are saved by looking in faith to the crucified Savior.

John 3:16 says God loved the world so much that He gave His only begotten Son, so that whoever believes in Him will not perish but have everlasting life. It shows that salvation flows from God's love and His gift of His Son. The word 'whoever' means the offer is open to anyone, not just the worthy, the clean, or the Jews. The door to salvation is as wide as that word, and the condition is believing in Him.

John 3:17 says God did not send His Son to condemn the world but so the world might be saved through Him; He came with a cross, not a gavel. Yet verse 19 explains why people still face condemnation: the light has come, but men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil. The problem is never that the light is too dim but that people close their eyes to it. Whoever comes to the light shows that he is born of God.

The new birth is not a touch-up or turning over a new leaf but a change from the inside out. The lesson uses the caterpillar, which enters a cocoon and comes out not as a better caterpillar but as a creature with wings. In the same way, the old nature is put to death and a new nature alive to God is given. R. A. Torrey's conversion, from despair and unbelief to a life that led thousands to Christ, illustrates this Spirit-worked change.

The woman thought only of the water in Jacob's well, but Jesus was offering the gift of God, which is ultimately Himself and eternal life. Well water satisfies for a few hours and then you are thirsty again. The water Christ gives becomes a fountain inside the person, springing up into everlasting life, so the one who drinks it will never thirst again. It does not run out or need to be rationed; it overflows.

Jesus crossed three walls that a respectable rabbi would not climb. She was a Samaritan, and Jews and Samaritans despised each other; she was a woman, and teachers did not speak with women in public; and she was known as a great sinner, with five past husbands and living with a man who was not her husband. Yet Jesus started the conversation Himself by asking for a drink. This shows that His grace reaches outsiders and those others consider hopeless cases.

The woman raised the old dispute over whether the right place to worship was the Samaritans' mountain or Jerusalem. Jesus lifted the question higher: because God is Spirit, true worship is not finally about the right mountain or building. It must come from the heart, by the Spirit, and according to the truth God has revealed. Worship is a matter of inward reality and truth, not location or ritual.

When the woman spoke of the coming Messiah, Jesus told her plainly, 'I who speak to you am He.' He had not said this so openly to anyone else. It is striking because she was a Samaritan, a woman, an outsider, and a sinner, meeting Him at a well at noon. The first person to hear Jesus openly name Himself Messiah was someone society rejected, showing His grace toward the least likely.

After meeting Jesus, the woman left her waterpot and ran into town to the very people who knew her reputation. She said, 'Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did. Could this be the Christ?' She had no training or method, just a personal testimony and an invitation. Many Samaritans believed because of her word, and then many more believed after hearing Jesus for themselves and called Him the Savior of the world.

The Divine Partnership means God provides salvation and the power of His Spirit, and then works through His people to accomplish His purpose. Philippians 2:13 says it is God who works in us both to will and to do. The lesson compares this to a garden: God gives life, sun, and rain, but the gardener must tend it. In John 4, Jesus sowed in one woman, and she carried the message to her village; one sows and another reaps, and both rejoice together while God gives the increase.

When the disciples urged Jesus to eat, He said His food was to do the Father's will and finish His work. Then He pointed to the Samaritans coming out of town toward Him and told the disciples to look at the fields already white for harvest. He meant people were ready to receive the gospel now, not at some later season. Because He had sown in one woman, a whole village was ripening, and the disciples were called to reap and share the joy.

The disciples were trained men who had been with Jesus, yet they went into the same town and came back with food but no converts; there is no sign they spoke to anyone. The woman had no training and a bad reputation, yet her excited testimony brought many to Jesus. The contrast shows that God uses grateful, willing witnesses more than qualifications. A person who has truly tasted the living water naturally overflows with it.

The lesson lists several kinds of evangelists: the mass evangelist like Billy Graham, the apologist or defender of the faith like Lee Strobel, Josh McDowell, and Nabeel Qureshi, and the serving evangelist like Barnabas. There is the tract evangelist like the paralyzed J. D. Fore, the timid evangelist like the man on George Street in Sydney asking one question, and the invitational evangelist like the Samaritan woman. The truth is that every believer is on the team; there is not just one kind of witness. Anyone who has tasted the living water can at least say 'come and see.'

Every person is made with a thirst that the world's wells, such as money, pleasure, approval, or relationships, cannot fill; they satisfy for a moment and then the dryness returns. The Samaritan woman had tried those wells many times. Jesus offered her Himself, and in Him alone are found both salvation and a real purpose for living. Like Niagara Falls that never stops pouring, His supply never runs dry.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle that all four Gospel writers recorded, which shows how important it was considered. It recalls Israel in the wilderness, when a huge crowd of former slaves had no food and no human solution, a God-sized problem. God answered then with manna, bread from heaven. In John 6 there is again a great crowd in an empty place with no food, and the same God provides, but this time Jesus goes on to say that He Himself is the Bread.

Philip calculated the cost and gave up, saying that even two hundred denarii, about eight months' wages, would not buy enough for each person to have a little. Andrew found a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish, the poor man's food, but asked what that was among so many. John notes that Jesus already knew what He would do. He let the problem grow in the disciples' eyes so they would learn that the answer was not in their arithmetic but in their Lord.

Jesus was moved with compassion for the crowd and healed their sick; the Gospels mention His compassion six times, and it was a flood in Him. The lesson rejects the idea that the Old Testament God is harsh while Jesus is kind, as if they were two different Gods. There is no difference between the Father and the Son; the Old Testament repeatedly speaks of God's compassion, and God was in Christ reconciling the world. The same heart that gave Israel manna fed the crowd by Galilee, and that compassion should now flow through us as His body.

Mary Reed was born in Ohio in 1858 and went to India, where she could not forget a forsaken colony of about five hundred lepers in the Himalayas. When she learned she had leprosy herself, she accepted it as a strange gift from God that would let her live among them. She served those outcasts for fifty-three years until she died among them in 1943. Her story shows Christ's compassion flowing through a surrendered life to people no one else would touch.

After everyone was full, the disciples gathered twelve baskets of leftovers from five loaves, more than there was at the beginning; this shows grace upon grace that never runs out. It also shows that God takes a small gift surrendered to Him and multiplies it. The widow of Zarephath gave her last flour and oil to the prophet first and never ran empty. Dr. Cook says he was not a natural preacher, but he offered God his small gift and learned that God multiplies it, so the work is for God's glory, not his own.

The crowd wanted to force Jesus to be king because He could fill their stomachs and end every shortage. Jesus withdrew to the mountain alone because He would not be crowned on human terms or for human appetites; His kingdom comes from the Father, and He will reign in God's time. 'The Creator is no man's debtor' means God gives because He is good, not because we can corner or control Him. It warns against wanting Jesus for what He gives rather than for Himself.

That evening the disciples were rowing across the lake in the dark against a storm, getting nowhere, when they saw Jesus walking on the water. They were terrified until He said, 'It is I; do not be afraid.' In Greek His words are literally 'I AM,' the name of God, showing that He is Lord over the sea He created. As soon as they received Him into the boat, they were immediately at the land where they were going.

Jesus told the crowd they were not seeking Him because of the signs but because they had eaten the loaves and were full. He urged them not to labor for food that perishes but for food that lasts to eternal life. When they pointed to Moses and the manna, He said the manna was only a shadow and that the true Bread from heaven had now come and was standing before them. Then He declared, 'I am the bread of life.'

The real hunger of our time is a spiritual hunger for God. People try to fill that emptiness with food, sex, money, and recognition, but each leaves the soul as hollow as before. Augustine chased those things in his early years and was still starving. He finally concluded that God made us for Himself and our hearts are restless until they find their rest in Him.

In John 6:51 Jesus said the bread He would give is His flesh, given for the life of the world, pointing to the cross and to feeding on Him by faith. Many disciples found this too hard, turned back, and stopped following Him. When Jesus asked the Twelve if they would leave too, Peter answered, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.' The lesson says that just as the boy gave his loaves and the disciples passed them on, we must carry the Bread we have received to a hungry, perishing world.

Jesus did not say He would show us a light or teach about it; He said He Himself is the light, greater than the sun because He lights the depths of the soul. He promised that whoever follows Him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. Following Him means being a disciple, a learner under His discipline and trained in the truth by the Master, not just an admirer. The early believers called themselves followers of 'the Way' because they fixed their eyes on Him and walked by His light.

Light and darkness cannot share a room; one match in a cellar drives the dark away. When Jesus came, His light exposed people's hearts, but the darkness did not comprehend it, and people loved darkness because their deeds were evil and they hated having them exposed. The religious leaders thought keeping and tightening rules made them righteous, but the Light showed how far short their hearts fell. The Light also kindles: those who follow Christ reflect His light to others, like a small lighthouse flame magnified by mirrors.

No one can see God, but in Jesus the invisible God is made visible. In Him the holiness known from the Old Testament is joined with a love and mercy people had hardly dared to see. Regarding the law, He did not come to abolish it but to fulfill it. He also exposed the leaders' mistaken idea that a list of rules could contain God's whole will.

When the leaders mocked that He was not yet fifty and could not have seen Abraham, Jesus said, 'Before Abraham was, I AM.' He did not say 'I was,' but used 'I AM,' the name God revealed to Moses at the burning bush, the name of the eternal, self-existent God. So He claimed both to exist before Abraham and to bear the divine name. The leaders understood He was claiming to be God, and since they would not bow, they picked up stones to kill Him for blasphemy. They were right about the claim but wrong about the Man.

In John 8 Jesus is the monogenes, the one unique Son who shares the Father's very nature, unlike believers who are adopted into God's family. From His mother He took a true humanity, so He could grow weary, thirst, and die. From the Father He has wisdom and power no man ever had, so He astonished teachers as a boy, knew strangers' secret lives, healed, walked on the sea, and rose from the dead. He is fully God and fully man in one Person, and His claim to equality with God, including 'before Abraham was, I AM,' is what made the leaders want to kill Him.

The disciples assumed, as their culture did, that suffering like blindness from birth must be punishment for someone's sin, either the man's or his parents'. Jesus rejected that assumption and said neither had sinned, but the blindness existed so that the works of God would be revealed in him. Not every sorrow is a sentence for sin. God can use suffering as a stage for displaying His glory and power.

Saying 'As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world,' Jesus spat on the ground, made clay, anointed the blind man's eyes, and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam, which means 'Sent.' The man went down in darkness and came back seeing. The sign shows Jesus doing literally what He claimed: as the Light of the world He gave sight to a man who had never seen. It echoes the Creator who once said, 'Let there be light.'

At first the healed man simply calls Jesus 'a man called Jesus' and holds to what he knows: 'though I was blind, now I see.' Under pressure from the Pharisees he says, 'He is a prophet.' Then, despite their threats, he insists that if this Man were not from God He could do nothing. After he is thrown out of the synagogue, Jesus finds him and asks if he believes in the Son of God; he says, 'Lord, I believe,' and worships Him. His eyes opened in an instant, but his heart came into the light step by step.

The man born blind gained physical sight instantly and spiritual sight gradually, ending in worship, while the Pharisees, who had perfectly good eyes, grew darker the more they resisted. Jesus said He came so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind. When the Pharisees asked if they were blind too, He said that if they admitted blindness they would have no sin, but because they claimed to see, their sin remained. The only people the Light cannot help are those who insist they need no help.

The 'I AM' sayings echo the divine name God gave Moses, so each one is a claim to deity as well as a picture of what Jesus gives. In John He says He is the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine. Together they show He alone satisfies, enlightens, gives access to God, protects and lays down His life, conquers death, is the only way to the Father, and gives fruitful life to those joined to Him. The absolute 'before Abraham was, I AM' makes the claim to be God explicit.

John's Gospel is built like a trial: the claim on the table is that Jesus is God in the flesh, and John calls witness after witness so the reader, like a juror, can weigh the evidence and reach a verdict. John 20:31 says he wrote so that we may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name. Under Jewish law a matter had to be established by two or three witnesses, since a single witness can be mistaken. Jesus offers far more than two, and they all agree, which leaves the reader without excuse.

At the pool of Bethesda a man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, and Jesus healed him with a word on the Sabbath. Instead of rejoicing, the leaders were furious. John 5:18 says they sought all the more to kill Him because He not only broke the Sabbath but also called God His Father, making Himself equal with God. Jesus did not deny that charge; He answered it by calling His witnesses.

Jesus said He had a greater witness than John the Baptist: the works the Father gave Him to finish testify that the Father sent Him. His signs were not just wonders but sworn evidence of His identity. Beyond the works, the Father Himself who sent Him has testified of Him. The Father is the second witness the Law required and the highest witness of all.

The leaders searched the Scriptures thinking that in them they had eternal life, but Jesus said those very Scriptures testify about Him. They had the witness in their hands and refused to hear it. He also said that He would not need to accuse them before the Father, because Moses, whom they trusted, accuses them, since Moses wrote about Him. So the lawgiver they relied on was actually a witness against their unbelief.

The Law required two witnesses, and Jesus named Himself and the Father, but Dr. Cook adds a third for today: the Holy Spirit. Jesus promised that the Helper, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, would testify of Him (John 15:26). The Spirit has never stopped testifying of Christ, both through the Scriptures He inspired and in the heart of every believer He has made alive. The same Spirit who convinced us that Jesus is Lord is a living witness today.

When the Pharisees said His self-testimony was not valid, Jesus said it was true because He knew where He came from and where He was going, while they did not. A liar can be caught because he is inventing, but the Son speaks from firsthand knowledge of heaven, the Father, and His own eternal origin. He also said He did not stand alone: He and the Father together are the two witnesses the Law requires. So His testimony rests on a Son who cannot be mistaken about Himself and a Father who confirms every word.

The Samaritan woman, after Jesus told her everything she had done, ran into her town and said, 'Come, see a Man who told me all that I ever did. Could this be the Christ?' Many believed because of her word. The man born blind, brought before the council and pressured to deny his Healer, said, 'One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.' His parents dodged the question out of fear, but he testified anyway and was cast out of the synagogue. Neither was a trained theologian; each simply told what they had seen of Christ.

The nobleman's son was dying, and Jesus healed him from a distance. The father did not keep that mercy to himself; he believed, and his whole household believed with him (John 4:53). Mary Magdalene, a woman from whom seven demons had gone out, was weeping at the empty tomb when she met the risen Lord. She became the first witness of the resurrection, running to the disciples to say, 'I have seen the Lord!'

After so many sure witnesses, Jesus told the leaders, 'You are not willing to come to Me that you may have life.' The tragedy is that the problem was never a lack of evidence. It was an unwilling will; they simply refused to come. Unbelief, then, is often a moral and volitional refusal rather than an intellectual difficulty.

Having set all the witnesses before us, the Baptist, the works, the Father, the Scriptures, Moses, the Spirit, and many changed lives, John asks for our verdict. The only honest verdict is that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing we have life in His name. Then believers are called to take the stand themselves, for Jesus said, 'You shall be witnesses to Me' (Acts 1:8). Like the Samaritan woman and the blind man, we do not need cleverness, only firsthand knowledge of Christ to say 'come and see' or 'now I see.'

Isaiah 53:6 says all of us like sheep have gone astray, each turning to his own way. Sheep need more care than any other farm animal: they are timid, stubborn, quick to wander, and a lost sheep cannot find its way home. Phillip Keller's restless fence-crawling ewe, who led other sheep out to barren ground, pictures how we wander and lead others astray. Because we are helpless and lost on our own, we desperately need a shepherd to guide, protect, and bring us home.

In the warm season, shepherds kept the flock at night in a rough hillside fold, a space surrounded by a low stone wall with one opening but no gate. The shepherd lay down across that opening, so no sheep could get out and no wolf could get in except over his body; he literally was the door. Jesus said, 'I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture.' The sheep go in for safety at night and out to pasture in the morning, and both ways are through Him.

Jesus said the thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy, but He came so His sheep may have life and have it more abundantly. The thieves and robbers were the false leaders who set themselves up as gatekeepers to God and shut people out of the kingdom they claimed to guard. The thief takes from the sheep for his own benefit. The Shepherd gives, and gives overflowing life.

Jesus says He is the door, not one of many doors, and Ephesians 2:18 says it is through Him that we have access to the Father. The lesson's dream of searching for hours around a house in the freezing cold and finding only one open door pictures this: there is only one way in. Any road that claims to reach God while going around this Door falls short. That is why He called false leaders thieves and robbers, because they offered other ways and actually kept people out.

In Israel a shepherd stayed with his flock for years and gave each sheep a descriptive name like 'Brown-leg' or 'Black-ear,' calling each by its own name. Jesus says He knows His sheep and is known by them. Throughout Scripture God called people by name, like Abraham, Moses, and Samuel. This means believers are not numbers or faces in a crowd but are personally known by the God who placed the stars.

Sheep learn their shepherd's voice by living with him day after day, and they will not follow a stranger. A traveler near Bethlehem saw two flocks sheltered in one cave; in the morning one shepherd simply gave his call, and only his sheep came running after him. Jesus says, 'My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.' Believers learn to recognize God's voice, as the man freed from drink and drugs did when he heard an inner voice tell him to turn from the world and knew it was God.

The hireling works only for wages; the sheep are not his, so when he sees the wolf coming he leaves them and runs because he does not care about them. The good shepherd owns the sheep and was born to the task, so he puts himself between them and danger. Some shepherds in the Holy Land actually fought to the death defending their flocks from raiders. Jesus is the good shepherd who gives His life for the sheep.

The word 'good' here means more than skilled or kind; it means good in the very nature of the thing, beautiful and ideal, the model others can safely follow. That goodness is not something Jesus achieved but what He is, so calling Him good in this full sense amounts to calling Him God. He gives His life for the sheep, and He said no one takes it from Him; He lays it down of Himself. His death was not an accident or a defeat but a deliberate sacrifice that shows how far the Father would go to gather His sheep.

Jesus gives His sheep eternal life, they will never perish, and no one can snatch them out of His hand. Their security does not depend on their weak grip on Him but on His almighty grip on them. What He bought at so great a price He does not lose. He then said, 'I and My Father are one,' which the leaders understood as a claim to be God, so they picked up stones again.
Christ does not keep His sheep; they can be snatched from His hand

A trained orator recited Psalm 23 so beautifully that the audience applauded, but when an old man recited the same words, the room fell silent in prayer. The orator admitted that the difference was that he knew the Psalm, but his friend knew the Shepherd. The point is that admiring the Shepherd from outside the fold is not enough. We must enter through the Door and have a personal relationship with Christ, knowing Him and being known by Him.

The tragedy: Lazarus, a man loved by Jesus and in the prime of life, fell sick and died, and the loss was real for his family. The trial: Jesus deliberately stayed two more days, saying the sickness was for God's glory, so the family and disciples had to trust Him in the dark without understanding. The tears: at Bethany, surrounded by mourning, Jesus wept, entering into the grief of those He loved. The triumph: He declared, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' and called Lazarus out of the tomb after four days, showing His power over death.

Cook says death is a tragedy even when we are sure we will see the person again, because the loss is real and the absence hurts. He speaks from experience: he had almost two years to say goodbye to his first wife, and it was still perhaps the hardest thing he ever faced, and he remembers his mother's cry when his baby niece died. Death is a real enemy, and Scripture never asks us to pretend otherwise. Hope in the resurrection does not erase the pain of separation.

When Jesus heard Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days instead of hurrying. He said the sickness was not unto death but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God would be glorified through it. Lazarus died within God's permissive will, allowed for a purpose no one could yet see. The delay set the stage for a far greater display of His power, raising a man four days dead, so that God would be glorified and faith strengthened.

Trials ask us to trust God in the dark before we can see the reason, and it is only when faith is tested that it grows. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed, but God answered, 'My grace is sufficient for you.' William Sangster could not explain to his three-year-old son why he had to have a painful surgery, so he said, 'You must trust my love.' God often leaves us in that place, unable to see why, called simply to trust the love of a Father who will make it plain one day.

'Jesus wept' is the shortest verse in the Bible but one of the fullest. Jesus knew He would raise Lazarus within the hour, yet He still wept, not for Lazarus but for the grief of those He loved and for a world under the shadow of death. He did not stand above their sorrow but entered into it. This shows that God is not a stranger to our grief and models Romans 12:15, weeping with those who weep.

Martha believed Lazarus would rise at the last day, a distant future hope. Jesus brought the resurrection into the present and into His own Person: 'I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live, and whoever lives and believes in Me shall never die.' Resurrection is not first an event or a doctrine but Christ Himself. To have Him is to have a life that death cannot end, and He asks each of us, 'Do you believe this?'

After the stone was removed, despite Martha's protest that the body would smell after four days, Jesus cried with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come forth!' and Lazarus came out still bound in grave clothes. It shows Jesus' absolute authority over death; it has been said that if He had not named Lazarus, every grave might have emptied at His voice. In that moment every doubt was buried. It also foreshadows the day when the same voice will call every believer out of the grave by name.

After raising Lazarus, Jesus told the people to unbind him and let him go. Only Christ can give life, but He let the community remove the grave clothes and welcome Lazarus back. The church's part is similar: we help those newly alive in Christ get free of the bindings of their past by teaching, encouraging, and walking with them. Christ gives the life; we help the new believer live it out.

Everyone secretly fears death, but this sign shows that Jesus has power over the grave itself, and the One who can conquer death can take away every fear. Jesus pictured death as sleep. Like a tired child who falls asleep on the couch and wakes in his own bed because his father carried him there, the believer falls asleep in death and wakes safe where the Father has carried him. The grave becomes a doorway rather than a wall, as shown by the man buried with his finger on John 3:16.

The raising of Lazarus is the greatest sign because it is greater than water into wine, feeding the five thousand, or opening blind eyes: Lazarus had been dead and buried four days, and Jesus showed power over death itself. Death is the deepest question any religion must answer, and here Jesus answers it. When Martha hesitated about opening the tomb, Jesus said, 'Did I not say that if you would believe you would see the glory of God?' This calls us to trust and obey Him even when it seems hopeless, so that we too will see His glory.

Throughout John, Jesus' enemies could not seize Him because His hour had not yet come. In John 12 some Greeks who came to worship at the feast asked Philip, 'Sir, we would see Jesus,' and when Jesus heard it He said the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Their request expresses the deep human longing for a Person, not a doctrine or a debate. The arrival of Gentile seekers signaled that the world was beginning to seek Him, and that the hour of His death and glory had arrived.

Jesus said that unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies it produces much grain. A seed kept safe on a shelf stays a single lonely seed; only by being buried and broken does it become a harvest. In the same way, the road to Jesus' glory and to a world full of redeemed people went through His death. The cross was not the failure of His hour but the very means of His glory.

Jesus applied the same principle to His followers: whoever loves his life will lose it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. A clenched fist keeps nothing, but the open, surrendered hand bears fruit. We naturally want glory without a cross and a crown without surrender, but there is no shortcut around the buried seed. The French Christian widow who took a Jewish woman's papers and died in a camp in her place, saying it was the least she could do since Christ had done more for her, shows a life laid down that bore fruit in someone else.

Jesus admitted His soul was troubled, but instead of asking to be saved from the hour, He prayed, 'Father, glorify Your name.' A voice came from heaven saying, 'I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.' The crowd heard it differently: some said it thundered, others that an angel spoke, showing that hearts hear God according to their openness to Him. The voice revealed that the Father would be glorified in the Son, both through the signs already done and through the coming cross.

Glory is the holiness of God made visible. No one could look at it directly; even Moses saw only its afterglow. But John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory as of the only begotten of the Father. In Jesus, and most of all in His self-giving death, God's hidden glory comes out into the open where people can see it.

On the night He was betrayed, while the disciples argued about who was the greatest, no servant was there to wash their dusty feet and none of them would do it. Jesus, knowing He had come from God and was going to God, got up from supper, took off His outer garment, tied a towel around Himself, and washed their feet. The Son of God knelt at the dirty feet of fishermen just hours before the cross. This shows that true greatness is humble service, and it is the very glory the Greeks had asked to see.

The world measures greatness by how many people work for you, but the Lord measures it by how many people you serve. Jesus taught that the greatest among His followers must be their servant. Believers in China told a missionary that what won them to Christ was not miracles or teaching but Jesus washing feet, because they had never known a God who stooped with a towel and basin. So when we are tempted to stand on our dignity or rights, we should remember the Lord of glory on His knees.

Jesus said that since He, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, they ought to wash one another's feet, because He had given them an example. It is a command to humble, practical service toward others. Today we wash feet when we care for the sick, feed the poor, honor aging parents, drive a neighbor to the doctor, or open our homes. Greatness in the kingdom wears an apron.

Jesus gave a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. The standard is His own love, which laid down His life and took up the towel. By this love everyone will know that we are His disciples. The world that wants to see Jesus will see Him most clearly not in our arguments or buildings but in a people who lay down their lives for one another.

In this hour God's glory is shown not by an army or throne but by a grain of wheat that dies, a voice from heaven, and a towel and basin. Jesus is glorified through His death on the cross and through humble service like washing feet. This reverses the world's idea of glory. It calls us first to look to the grain that died for us, and then to take up the towel: surrender our lives, serve others, and love one another as He loved us.

On the night before the cross the disciples' hearts were breaking, so Jesus told them not to be troubled but to believe in God and in Him. He said that in His Father's house are many dwelling places, that He was going to prepare a place for them, and that He would come again and take them to be with Him. Heaven is a real place, the believer's true home, not wishful thinking. Like the boy in the attic who received his grandfather's letter saying 'Come home,' believers can look forward to the day Christ calls them home.

When Thomas asked how they could know the way, Jesus did not give him a map but a Person: 'I am the way.' The opposite of the way is being lost, and not every road reaches God no matter how sincerely it is traveled. Jesus taught that there are only two roads, the broad one leading to destruction and the narrow one that few find. He said no one comes to the Father except through Him, so every road that tries to go around Him falls short.

Jesus is not merely a teacher of true things; He is the Truth in person, so to know Him is to know what is real. He is also the Life. A person without Him is not just uninformed or unlucky but spiritually dead, alive to the world yet dead to God. Only Christ can make such a person truly alive, giving abundant life now and eternal life forever. Josh McDowell's story shows the point: the answer was not religion but Jesus Christ Himself.

This is the last of the seven I AM sayings. Even the Great Vine near London, centuries old with huge branches and many grapes, is only a picture; Jesus is the true vine, the real source of spiritual life. The Father is the vinedresser, who is much more than a farmer. He knows each vine intimately, what it needs and when, and exactly where and at what angle to cut, so that it bears fruit.

Every branch that bears fruit the Father prunes so that it will bear more fruit. Pruning is not punishment but love with a knife. Sometimes He cuts away what is clearly dead, but often He cuts away even good and better things so we can have the best. It hurts but it helps, as with Paul's thorn, which God did not remove but used, saying, 'My grace is sufficient for you,' to make him more fruitful.

'Abide' is the verb behind the word 'abode,' a dwelling place. To abide in Christ is more than knowing facts about Him or even praying; it is living with Him in a close, family relationship, aware of Him beside us every moment. Like a phone that must stay plugged in to charge, we receive life and power only while we stay connected to the Vine. The Polish believers who stayed on their knees after Stuart Briscoe's sermon show the seriousness of making sure we are abiding.

Jesus said He is the vine and we are the branches, and without Him we can do nothing. A branch cut off from the vine cannot produce anything by itself. Apart from Christ we can do nothing of eternal value, no matter how busy we are. But when we abide in Him, His life flows through us and fruit comes.

Many assume a real Christian will produce fruit automatically, but Jesus says fruit comes only by abiding in Him. Abiding itself is not automatic either, or He would not have needed to command it; that same night all the disciples, especially Peter, failed to abide. Fruit comes as we stay connected to the Vine and His life flows through us. When there is no fruit, it is an attachment problem, and the cure is not to quit but to clear away sin and abide afresh.

Fruit includes evangelism and winning souls, but it is more than that. Believers bear fruit by using the gifts God has given them, such as teaching, hospitality, mercy, and prayer. Above all they bear the fruit of the Spirit from Galatians 5: love, joy, peace, and the rest. When the world sees people marked by this fruit, it sees something it cannot explain or produce, and all of it is for the Father's glory.

The two sayings answer the soul's two deepest questions. 'I am the way' tells us how to get home to the Father: only through Christ. 'I am the true vine' tells us how to live until we get there: by abiding in Him so His life makes us fruitful. They call us first to come to the Father through the one Way, and then to stay close to the Vine and let His life bear fruit through us for the Father's glory.

The disciples saw His leaving as pure loss, but Jesus said that unless He went away the Helper would not come, and if He went He would send Him. While on earth Jesus could be in only one place at a time, but through the Spirit He would be with every believer everywhere, always. So their grief had a purpose they could not yet see. Like a woman in labor, their sorrow would turn to joy.

Jesus calls the Spirit the Paraclete, which means Helper, Comforter, Advocate, literally 'one called alongside' to stand with us. He is 'another' Helper of the same kind as Jesus, God come close, and He is given not for a visit but to abide forever, dwelling with and in believers. He is the Spirit of truth, who teaches us all things and brings to remembrance what Jesus said. He is a divine Person, not a force or a feeling, who knows us, loves us, and never leaves.

Jesus said the Spirit of truth would testify of Him, and He has never stopped doing so, through the Scriptures He inspired and in believers' hearts. The Spirit also convicts the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, awakening consciences that are dead to God. He empowers ordinary believers to bear bold witness even when the world hates them as it hated Jesus. That is why the church has often grown fastest where it has suffered most.

Jesus said the Spirit would guide His people into all truth and would glorify Him. The Spirit does not advertise Himself; His work is to point to Christ. This is the key to recognizing the Spirit's true work. A life truly filled with the Spirit will not draw attention to itself or to spectacular signs but will point others to Jesus.

Jesus told the disciples they would weep and mourn while the world rejoiced, but their grief would turn to joy. He compared it to a woman in labor whose pain is real but turns to joy when the child is born. The joy He promised is one no one can take away. This reflects the pattern of faith: we are often asked to trust the Father in the dark before the reason is shown, as Dr. Cook learned in his own losses and in following God to a small, poor church that turned out to be the right path.

We often want God to lay out His whole plan at once, like a machine giving an instant answer, but He rarely works that way. Jesus told the disciples He had many things to say that they could not bear yet, so He gave them light for the next step. God is not training slaves who follow blind orders but sons and daughters who grow into the mind of Christ. The process of seeking His will over time shapes us, as God works in us to will and to do for His good pleasure.

In John 17, on the eve of His sacrifice, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and intercedes for His people, which is the work of a high priest. He prays first for Himself, that the Father would glorify the Son so the Son may glorify Him. Then He prays for His disciples, asking the Father to keep them from the evil one and sanctify them. Finally He prays for all future believers. He still intercedes for us before the Father's throne.

Jesus defined eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. Eternal life is not first a place or a long span of days but a relationship of knowing God. For His disciples He did not ask that they be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one. He prayed, 'Sanctify them by Your truth; Your word is truth,' meaning they would be set apart and made holy through God's word.

Jesus said He was praying not only for the eleven but for all who would believe in Him through their word, so every believer since was included in that prayer. He asked that they all be one, just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. This unity is not forced uniformity or a mere organization but a shared life that reflects the oneness of the Father and Son. Its purpose is evangelistic: so that the world may believe the Father sent Him.

Jesus promised, 'I will not leave you orphans,' and gave two gifts to prove it. The first is the Spirit, the Helper, God with us and in us, who teaches, convicts, comforts, and glorifies Christ through us. The second is His High-Priestly Prayer, in which He holds His people before the Father and continues to intercede for us. Together they mean that no matter our confusion, sorrow, or the world's hostility, we are not alone and not forgotten.

After the supper Jesus went to Gethsemane, prayed in agony, and yielded to the Father's will. Judas, one of His own, led soldiers with torches and weapons to arrest Him, a deep betrayal by a trusted friend. But when they said they were looking for Jesus of Nazareth, He answered, 'I am He,' and they drew back and fell to the ground. When Peter drew a sword, Jesus told him to put it away, asking, 'Shall I not drink the cup which My Father has given Me?' He went to the cross by His own choice, not because He was overpowered.

The soldiers mocked the idea that this beaten man could be a king by giving Him cruel versions of royal symbols: a crown of thorns, a faded purple robe thrown over His flogged back, and a reed for a scepter. Pilate then brought Him out and said, 'Behold the Man!' What looked like the humiliation of a criminal, John wants us to see as a coronation. The mockery unknowingly told the truth that Jesus is the King.

When Pilate asked, 'Shall I crucify your King?', the chief priests answered, 'We have no king but Caesar,' and Jesus was led to Golgotha. Pilate fastened a sign over the cross in three languages, 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,' and refused to change it: 'What I have written, I have written.' The deepest irony became the deepest truth: the cross was His throne. By not saving Himself, as the mockers demanded, He saves us, reigning from the cross for sinners like Rembrandt, who painted himself among the crucifiers.

'It is finished' was not the gasp of a defeated man saying 'I am finished,' but the shout of a victor. The word, tetelestai, was what a merchant stamped on a settled bill: Paid in Full. It means the entire work of redemption Jesus came to do was complete, with nothing to add and nothing still owed. From that finished work flows every forgiveness we will ever receive, sufficient even for someone like R. A. Torrey in his darkest hour.

John says Jesus bowed His head and gave up His spirit, which shows that no one took His life from Him. As the Good Shepherd had said, He laid it down of Himself. His death was not something done to Him against His will but a deliberate, voluntary act. This matches His willingness in the garden, where He chose to drink the Father's cup.

Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and found the stone rolled away. Weeping and thinking the body had been stolen, she did not recognize the risen Lord standing before her until He spoke her name, 'Mary.' She was a woman whose life He had rescued, and she became the first witness of the resurrection. Jesus sent her to carry the news to the apostles themselves.

Thomas refused to believe the other disciples, saying that unless he saw the nail marks he would not believe. Eight days later the risen Christ appeared among them and offered Thomas His wounded hands. Thomas fell before Him and confessed, 'My Lord and my God!', the great confession of the whole Gospel. Jesus answered that Thomas believed because he saw, but blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe, a blessing that reaches us today.

Peter had denied Jesus three times beside a fire, and by the Sea of Galilee he met Him again beside another fire. Three times Jesus asked, 'Do you love Me?', and three times Peter, grieved and humbled, said yes. Each time Jesus gave back his calling: 'Feed My sheep.' The public failure was answered by a public restoration, showing that the risen Lord restores those who fail Him and makes them pillars of His church.

The resurrection shows that in Christ failure is not fatal, life is not futile, and death is not final. Peter's restoration and the story of George Smith, a Moravian missionary who won only one woman, was expelled, and died praying, yet whose ministry led to over thirteen thousand believers a century later, show that God redeems apparent failure. The empty tomb, Jesus' many appearances including to more than five hundred, and the disciples' willingness to die for what they saw answer Job's question 'If a man dies, shall he live again?' with a resounding yes.

John 20:31 says these things were written so that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing we may have life in His name. The whole Gospel has worked like a courtroom, calling witness after witness: John the Baptist, the signs, the Father, the Scriptures, the Spirit, and the empty tomb. Having shown the King crowned, crucified, finished, and risen, John places the verdict in each reader's hands. To all who receive Him and believe, He gives the right to become children of God and eternal life.

Matthew starts with a genealogy because he wants to settle who Jesus is before telling anything He did; the list shows that God had been working toward this child for two thousand years, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations. Calling Him Son of David means He is the rightful heir to David's throne, the promised King whose kingdom will never end. Calling Him Son of Abraham means He is the one through whom God's promise to bless all the families of the earth comes true, so His blessing reaches the Gentile nations and not only Israel.

Matthew names four women, which was unusual since Jewish genealogies normally traced only fathers, and he skips the great matriarchs. He names Tamar, who deceived Judah; Rahab, the Gentile harlot of Jericho; Ruth, a Moabite from a people with a troubled history with Israel; and Bathsheba, 'the wife of Uriah,' which recalls David's sin. Their presence shows that grace runs through the Messiah's family line: the Savior was not ashamed to be born among sinners and outsiders. No one's past puts them beyond the reach of His family.

The name Jesus means 'the LORD saves,' and the angel explains that He will save His people from their sins, which tells us His mission: not only to teach or be admired, but to rescue from the deepest bondage, sin. Immanuel, from Isaiah 7:14, means 'God with us,' and it declares His identity as God Himself come to dwell among His people. Together the names say who He is and what He came to do: God in the flesh who has come near in order to save.

Isaiah 7:14 was first spoken to King Ahaz, who was threatened by an enemy alliance and was tempted to rely on Assyria instead of the LORD; when he hypocritically refused to ask for a sign, God gave one anyway. That sign had a real fulfillment in Ahaz's own day, probably in the birth of a child whose growth marked God's deliverance, since a sign seven hundred years off would have meant little to him. Yet the words reached further to their full fulfillment in Jesus, conceived by the Holy Spirit of a virgin, who alone is truly Immanuel, God with us. This is the typological, double-fulfillment reading many evangelicals hold.

Hosea 11:1 originally looked back to the Exodus, when God called the nation of Israel, His son, out of Egypt. Matthew sees it fulfilled again when the child Jesus returns from Egypt after Herod's death, because Jesus is the true Son who retraces Israel's path. This is recapitulation: Jesus relives Israel's story and gets it right. Israel wandered and failed in the wilderness for forty years, but Jesus in His forty days of temptation resisted the tempter exactly where the nation had fallen.

The Magi were wise men from the East, Gentile foreigners, who followed a star to Bethlehem seeking the one born King of the Jews so they could worship Him. Their visit shows that Jesus is the Son of Abraham through whom the nations are blessed, since outsiders are the first to seek Him while Jerusalem stays indifferent. It also shows He is a King worthy of worship, as their gifts declare. Already at His birth the nations are being drawn to Him.

Matthew puts two kings next to each other. Jesus is the King who comes to save His people, while Herod is the king who, troubled by the news, guards his throne at any cost. Herod tries to use the Magi as informants and, when outwitted, orders the slaughter of Bethlehem's baby boys, fulfilling Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping. The contrast shows that from the start the true King's coming is met by the violence of a world that loves its own power.

The Magi brought gold, frankincense and myrrh, and the lesson says each gift preaches a small sermon. Gold is tribute fit for a king, honoring Jesus as King. Frankincense is incense used in worship offered to God, pointing to His deity. Myrrh was a spice used to anoint the dead, foreshadowing His death on the cross even at the cradle.

Matthew repeatedly says events happened so that Scripture might be fulfilled: the virgin birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, the birth in Bethlehem and flight to Egypt fulfill the prophets and Hosea 11:1, the slaughter of the children echoes Jeremiah, and the move to Nazareth fulfills 'He shall be called a Nazarene.' Each fulfillment ties Jesus' early life to the Old Testament story. Together they form one message: the long history from Abraham through David has reached its goal in this child, the promised Messiah and true Israel.

Before any preaching or miracle, Unit 1 establishes that Jesus is the promised King and God Himself come among us. He is the Son of David, the rightful King; the Son of Abraham, through whom the nations are blessed; Jesus, who saves His people from their sins; and Immanuel, God with us. He is also the true Israel who fulfills His people's story. Because of this identity everyone must decide, like the Magi or like Herod, what they will do with Him.

John the Baptist was the prophet who appeared in the wilderness of Judea, dressed in camel's hair and eating locusts and wild honey, and baptized people in the Jordan as they confessed their sins. His message was 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Matthew identifies him as the voice crying in the wilderness from Isaiah 40:3, the herald sent ahead to prepare the way of the LORD, just as a herald went before an ancient king. His whole purpose was to point people past himself to the One coming after him.

The Pharisees and Sadducees trusted their descent from Abraham as if their pedigree secured them before God, but John insisted that a bloodline cannot repent; only a person can. True repentance is not just regret or a good resolution but a turning away from sin and back to God. Such turning shows itself in fruit, which is why John demanded 'fruits worthy of repentance' and warned that the axe was already at the root of fruitless trees. In the same way, a Christian upbringing or church membership cannot replace personal repentance, because God has no grandchildren.

John's baptism was with water unto repentance, a baptism of preparation in which people confessed that they needed cleansing. It could express the need but not meet it. The Coming One, mightier than John, would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, pouring out God's own life on His people. He also carries the winnowing fan of judgment, gathering the wheat and burning the chaff, so He both saves and judges.

Jesus had no sin to confess, so His baptism was not an act of personal repentance. When John objected, Jesus said it was fitting 'to fulfill all righteousness,' meaning He was doing what God required and taking His place beside the sinners He came to save. By stepping into the river with the guilty He identified Himself with His people from the very start of His ministry. It was the first step on a road that would end at the cross, where He would bear their sin.

When Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened and the Spirit of God descended on Him like a dove. At the same time the Father's voice spoke from heaven: 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' So in one moment the Son stood in the water, the Spirit descended, and the Father spoke. This shows one God in three Persons, not three gods, and it marks Jesus' anointing for His work.

Recapitulation means Jesus relives Israel's story and gets it right. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness and failed repeatedly by grumbling for bread, testing God and turning to idols; Jesus, led by the Spirit, fasts forty days in the wilderness and stands firm where the nation fell. That makes Him the true Israel, faithful where Israel was faithless. He is also the new Adam, because He does not yield to the tempter who ruined the first man.

First the devil told the hungry Jesus to turn stones into bread, using His power for His own appetite; Jesus answered from Deuteronomy that man lives not by bread alone but by every word from God's mouth. Second, on the pinnacle of the temple, Satan urged Him to throw Himself down and force God to rescue Him; Jesus replied, 'You shall not tempt the LORD your God.' Third, Satan offered all the kingdoms of the world if Jesus would worship him, a crown without the cross; Jesus said, 'Away with you, Satan,' because only God is to be worshiped and served. Each time He answered with 'It is written.'

After John was imprisoned, Jesus moved to Capernaum in Galilee by the sea. Matthew sees this as fulfilling Isaiah 9:1-2, which spoke of 'Galilee of the Gentiles,' where people sitting in darkness and the shadow of death would see a great light. Jesus Himself is that light, and it dawns in a region the world considered least important and close to the Gentiles. It again shows the King's reach to the nations.

Jesus began preaching with exactly John's words: 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' This shows that John was only the herald preparing the way, and now the herald's torch passes to the King Himself. It also shows continuity: the kingdom John announced as coming is now arriving in the person of Jesus. And it shows the kingdom requires the same response, a real turning to God.

Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus called the fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew, saying, 'Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men,' and they immediately left their nets. Then He called James and John, who immediately left their boat and their father Zebedee. Matthew stresses the word 'immediately,' echoing Joseph's ready obedience. It teaches that the King gathers His kingdom not by force but by His word that summons and hearts that respond, one call at a time.

When the crowds gathered, Jesus went up on a mountain and sat down to teach, the posture of a teacher. Matthew wants us to remember Moses going up Sinai and bringing down the law that formed Israel; now one greater than Moses gives the law of the kingdom of heaven, a kind of constitution for it. The sermon opens not with rules but with the Beatitudes, which describe the character of those who belong to God's kingdom. That character is paradoxical, blessing the poor, the mourning and the meek, the reverse of what the world calls blessed.

To be poor in spirit is to feel your deep spiritual destitution and to understand your nothingness before God, instead of leaning on your talents or education. Dr. Cook describes how, as a young Christian, his own abilities kept failing him until the Spirit showed him his real spiritual poverty and he began seeking the Lord Himself. The opposite is the Pharisee, who proudly thanked God that he was not like other men. There must be emptiness before fullness, and the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit because only empty hands reach out to be filled.

Biblical meekness is strength under control, great power harnessed and laid at God's feet. It is not weakness or being a doormat, as the joke group DOORMATS with its timid motto suggests. Moses confronting Pharaoh and Jesus driving the moneychangers from the temple were both meek, yet clearly not weak. Churchill's 'but I am a great man' shows the pride and blindness to one's faults that meekness lacks, while the surgeon who asked God's help before every operation shows humble dependence. The meek are promised that they will inherit the earth.

On their failed march to the South Pole in 1908, Shackleton and his companions were so starved that they talked about food every waking hour; that consuming craving is the picture of hungering for righteousness. Our problem is that we are too easily satisfied, and earthly appetites only produce more hunger, as with the rich young ruler. The righteousness meant here is right standing with God through justification and right living toward the helpless in compassion and obedience. The promise is that such people shall be filled, because God never starves an appetite He has given.

The unit defines mercy as refraining from harming or punishing those who are in our power and who deserve punishment. In the story, a mother begged Napoleon for her son's life even though he had twice committed a capital offense. When Napoleon said the son did not deserve mercy, she replied that it would not be mercy if he deserved it, and the emperor spared him. The lesson is that mercy is by nature undeserved; those who have received an ocean of mercy from God extend it to others and will themselves obtain mercy.

A little girl scrubbed a window but could not remove one dirty spot, because it was on the other side of the glass. Many people likewise work hard on the outside through education, fashion and cosmetics while the real dirt is inside, like the Pharisees who cleaned the outside of the cup. Being pure in heart means having an inner life that is cleansed and undivided, single-minded devotion to God. The promise, the greatest of the Beatitudes, is that they shall see God.

A peacemaker actively steps into conflict, takes the cost on himself, and makes peace where there was none, as in the Argentina-Chile arbitration commemorated by the Christ of the Andes. A peacemaker is not merely a peace-lover like Neville Chamberlain, whose appeasement bought a worse war, nor someone who keeps peace at any price, since Jesus also brought a sword. Peacemakers are called sons of God because that is exactly what God did for us in Christ: He bore the cost to make peace with us.

Salt preserves what would rot and gives flavor to what is bland, so believers are meant to hold back corruption and bring savor to the world. Light drives back darkness and shows the way, so believers make God's truth visible. But salt can lose its savor and a lamp can be hidden under a basket. Jesus therefore calls His people to let their light shine so others see their good works and glorify the Father in heaven; the kingdom character is not to be kept as private piety.

In Matthew 5:17 Jesus says He did not come to destroy the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them. Dr. Cook teaches that the Law was given to point us toward God's will, but it could never capture that will completely, since God's will includes what we should do as well as what we must not do. The commandments were never a means of salvation but a pointer to God's heart. Because Jesus knew the Father's will intimately, He got behind the laws to their intent, as in His 'You have heard... but I say to you' teaching on anger and lust. So our righteousness must exceed the Pharisees' surface rule-keeping with a heart-level righteousness.

Together the Beatitudes show that the kingdom's character is the reverse of the world's idea of the good life: poor in spirit, mourning, meek, hungry for righteousness, merciful, pure, peacemaking and willing to be persecuted. They are not eight entrance requirements we achieve to earn God's acceptance. Rather, they describe the character God's grace forms in those who already belong to Him. Feature by feature they are a portrait of Jesus Christ Himself, which the King is forming in His people.

Chapter 5 described who the citizens of the kingdom are, with the Beatitudes and the call to be salt and light. Chapters 6 and 7 turn to how they live, working that righteousness out in giving, prayer and fasting, in the use of money, in freedom from worry, in how we treat others, and finally in the decision between two foundations. The sermon refuses to let us admire the Beatitudes from a distance and presses them into ordinary daily life. The King wants obedience that runs deepest where only God is watching.

Jesus takes the three main acts of Jewish devotion, giving to the needy, prayer and fasting, and contrasts the hypocrites with the disciple. Hypocrites do them to be seen, and the applause of people is the only reward they get. The disciple gives without sounding a trumpet, prays in a closed room, and fasts without looking gloomy, doing it before the Father who sees in secret and will reward him. The key question is our audience: are we living for people's praise or before God alone?

Jesus tells us not to store up treasure on earth, where moth, rust and thieves destroy, but to store up treasure in heaven. The reason is that where your treasure is, there your heart will be also; the heart follows what we value, so treasure captures love. He adds that the eye is the lamp of the body, and a single, healthy eye fills life with light. No one can serve two masters, God and mammon; money is a useful servant but a ruinous lord. He is not condemning possessions but exposing a rival lordship, calling us to hold earthly things loosely.

Jesus says not to worry about life, pointing to the birds, which the Father feeds though they do not sow, and the lilies, which are clothed more gloriously than Solomon. If God cares for them, He will much more care for His children, and worry cannot add a single hour to life. Unlike the Gentiles who chase food and clothing, believers have a Father who knows what they need. So He commands, 'Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you,' taking each day as it comes.

'Judge not' forbids the hypocritical, condemning spirit that is harsh with others and blind to itself, pictured by a man with a plank in his eye trying to remove a speck from his brother's eye. We will be judged by the standard we use. It is not a ban on all discernment, since right after it Jesus says not to give what is holy to dogs or pearls to swine, which requires telling the difference. The disciple judges himself first and most strictly and then helps his brother humbly, as one beggar showing another where to find bread.

'Ask, seek, knock' teaches that God is a Father who delights to give. Jesus argues from lesser to greater: if evil human fathers do not give a stone to a son who asks for bread, how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask. Prayer is not prying open a reluctant hand. Out of that confidence comes the Golden Rule, to treat others the way we want to be treated, which sums up the Law and the Prophets in one sentence we can carry into every encounter.

There are two gates and roads: the narrow gate and hard way that lead to life and are found by few, and the wide gate and broad way that lead to destruction with many on them. There are two kinds of teachers: true ones and false prophets in sheep's clothing who are ravenous wolves inside, known by their fruits. And there are two claims: those who merely say 'Lord, Lord' and even point to mighty works, and those who actually do the Father's will. To the first Jesus will say, 'I never knew you.'

A wise man who hears Jesus' words and does them builds on the rock, while a foolish man who hears and does not do them builds on sand. From the outside both houses may look alike; the difference in foundation shows only when the storm, rain and floods come, and then the house on sand falls. The dividing line is not hearing but doing. The whole sermon ends here because it is not advice to admire but the King's authoritative word to obey, and the crowds were amazed that He taught with authority unlike the scribes.

Saying 'Lord, Lord' is only a verbal claim, and Jesus says only those who do the will of His Father will enter the kingdom. Some will even point to prophesying and mighty works done in His name, yet He will tell them, 'I never knew you; depart from Me.' Religious words and even religious activity are not the same as truly knowing Christ and obeying the Father. Real faith shows itself in obedience.

Matthew 6-7 shows that kingdom righteousness must be lived before God rather than for show: in secret devotion, in treasure laid up in heaven, in trust instead of worry, in humble rather than hypocritical judgment, in confident prayer and the Golden Rule. It ends with a series of choices between two ways, two kinds of teachers, two claims and two foundations. The response it calls for is not admiration but obedience: seeking first the kingdom and building our lives on doing what the King says.

Jesus gave this prayer when the disciples asked Him to teach them to pray, and He did not pray it for Himself, so it is better seen as the Disciples' or Model Prayer. It was not meant only to be memorized and recited but to be a pattern, with each phrase serving as a heading under which we bring our own concerns. It is short, in contrast to the vain repetitions of the heathen or the prophets of Baal, because the Father already knows our needs. Its six petitions are arranged with the first three about God and His glory (His name, kingdom and will) and the last three about our needs (daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation and evil).

All the pronouns in the prayer are plural, beginning with 'Our Father.' This teaches that when we pray we are part of God's worldwide family, so we have no right to ask for anything that would harm another member of it. That family includes young and old, rich and poor, every race and age, united in one fellowship across all differences. 'Our' also makes the prayer personal, because God is not an idol or object but someone we have a relationship with, as Enoch walked with God.

'Father' can mean mere paternity, the man biologically responsible for a birth who may never even see the child, or it can mean fatherhood, a relationship of love, confidence and trust. Christians believe God is Father in both senses: He is the source of all life, and through Jesus we can have an intimate, loving relationship with Him. This was unique, because the Stoics saw God as without feeling, the Epicureans as detached, and the Old Testament writers as splendid but terrible. Jesus prayed 'Abba, Father' in Gethsemane, and through Him we are adopted as sons.

'In heaven' is literally plural, 'in the heavens,' and it teaches that God is Spirit and is not confined to one place but is everywhere, creating, upholding and saving. A Russian cosmonaut said he did not see God in space, while some American astronauts saw Him clearly with spiritual eyes. Asking exactly where heaven is misses the point. It is better to think of the quality of life there, as Revelation 21:4 describes: no more tears, death, sorrow or pain, none of the things that bring grief to human life.

'Hallowed' means to be different and is related to holy, sanctified and saints. A temple is holy because it differs from other buildings, the Sabbath because it differs from other days, and a priest because he differs from other men. So the petition asks that God's name be treated differently from every other name. True worship recognizes that God is unlike us: He is spirit, all-powerful, all-knowing and good, while we are weak, ignorant and sinful. Before asking for things, we should be still and know that He is God, which leads to awe and reverence.

In Hebrew a name is more than a label; it means a person's nature and character as far as it has been revealed. So 'those who know Your name will trust You' means those who know what God is like will trust Him. Yahweh, the great 'I AM,' was revered so much that Jews would not pronounce it. But the lesson says the greatest reverence for God's name is shown by obeying His commandments, not by avoiding the word. Like the two men at the Lincoln statue in Chicago, one removing his hat and the other scribbling obscenities, people either honor or blaspheme His name.

A kingdom is a realm ruled by a king's word, not by elections or a congress. Israel once had no king but God until it demanded one from Samuel, and in the New Testament the Magi sought the King, His baptism was a kind of coronation, and He told Pilate His kingdom was not of this world. The kingdom is past, since Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are in it; present, since it is within or among us and the church is built on the rock; and still coming, since we still fall short of His glory. It is also spreading, as seen in the growth of the church in Africa, China and Iran.

We learn God's will through conscience, the inner voice that tells us to stop or urges us to do good; through circumstances, as when Albert Schweitzer read a misdelivered magazine about the Congo mission; through our talents, like the woman told she should sing in the choir; and through the counsel of others, like Thomas Carlyle's mother urging him to trust God and do right. The caution is that we try to learn everything at once, but God reveals His will like a kerosene lantern that lights only a few steps ahead. So we should ask what God wants us to do today, not demand the whole plan for our lives.

Some refuse to hear God's will, like the sick woman in Peter Marshall's story who realized she preferred her quiet bed; some reject it sadly, like the rich young ruler; and some respond in anger, as Beethoven supposedly died with clenched fists. The supreme example is Jesus in Gethsemane, sweating drops like blood yet praying, 'Not my will, but thine, be done.' We can trust God's will because He knows the future, because He knows what is best like a stained-glass window seen from inside, because His will is to bless as Joseph said what was meant for evil God meant for good, and because His will is sovereign, as Jonah learned.

The doxology is not in the oldest manuscripts and is best seen as an epilogue of praise echoing David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11. The kingdom is God's; the power is His, power we often fail to access, like the farmer who sawed by hand because he never pulled the chainsaw's cord, or the church Aquinas said could no longer say 'rise up and walk.' The glory is His, the manifestation of His holiness, pictured by the star R136a1, millions of times brighter than the sun, and by Lecrae's point that we are valuable because of whose name is on us. The guide's warning that on the summit the only safe place is on your knees reminds us the prayer frames life between God's fatherly nearness and His majesty.

The Sermon on the Mount ended with the crowds amazed that Jesus taught with authority, and chapters 8-9 show that same authority in action. Matthew groups about nine miracles in three sets, with teaching on discipleship in between, so that the King's works confirm His words. In them Jesus heals, calms the storm, casts out demons, forgives sins and raises the dead. All of it presses the disciples' question in the boat: 'Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?'

Jesus touched the leper, whom no one under the law would touch, and said 'I am willing; be cleansed'; His touch did not pick up defilement but gave cleansing. The Roman centurion understood authority and said Jesus need only speak a word and his servant would be healed, since he was not worthy to have Him under his roof. Jesus marveled that He had not found such faith even in Israel. Together they show the King's authority works by touch or by word, and the faith He looks for is humble trust in His word, even from a Gentile, a sign that many will come from east and west.

After Jesus healed Peter's mother-in-law and many others that evening, Matthew quoted Isaiah 53:4: 'He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.' This shows the healings are more than acts of kindness; they are signs pointing ahead to the cross. There the Suffering Servant would bear away the deepest sickness of all, sin. So each healing previews what His death would accomplish.

A great storm arose on the sea and the waves covered the boat while Jesus slept. The terrified disciples woke Him crying, 'Lord, save us! We are perishing!' He rebuked their little faith, then rebuked the winds and sea, and there was a great calm. The disciples marveled, 'Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?' In the Old Testament only the LORD rules the raging sea, so the miracle reveals that Jesus is God, the Lord of wind and wave.

When a paralyzed man was brought to Him, Jesus first said, 'Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you.' The scribes were scandalized because only God can forgive sins, and they were right, which is exactly the point Jesus was making about Himself. He then asked which is easier to say and healed the man so they would know the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins. The visible healing proved the invisible authority, showing that His deepest work is dealing with sin and guilt.

Jesus saw Matthew, a despised tax collector, at his booth and simply said, 'Follow Me,' and Matthew got up and followed. When Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners at Matthew's house, the Pharisees objected. Jesus answered that the healthy do not need a doctor but the sick do, and quoted 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' adding that He came to call sinners, not the righteous, to repentance. God values compassion toward people above the Pharisees' outward religious observance.

New wine ferments and expands, so it needs a fresh skin that can stretch; an old, dry, brittle wineskin will burst. The religion of Jesus' day had hardened in its rules, structures and thinking and could not contain the living newness He brought. The danger remains for churches: inflexible rules that measure faith by what people do not do, inflexible structures that say 'we never did it that way before,' and inflexible thinking that stops looking for new ways to reach people. Our standard is a Person, not rules; the Pharisees lifted up rules and broke people, while Jesus lifted up people and broke rules.

A ruler knelt and told Jesus his daughter had just died, trusting that if Jesus laid His hand on her she would live. On the way, a woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years touched the hem of His garment, believing that would heal her, and Jesus told her, 'Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well.' Then He went to the ruler's house, took the dead girl by the hand, and she arose. His authority reaches even into the grave, and both the woman and the father show that even small faith that comes to Jesus is not turned away.

Matthew 9 closes with two blind men healed, a mute man delivered, and growing opposition as the Pharisees claim He casts out demons by the ruler of demons. But Matthew ends on Jesus' heart: seeing the multitudes weary and scattered like sheep without a shepherd, He was moved with compassion. That compassion leads Him to tell the disciples that the harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few, so they should pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers. His authority is the power of a compassionate Shepherd-King.

Matthew 8-9 answers 'Who can this be?' by showing Jesus as the King with authority over disease, nature, demons, sin and death. He fulfills Isaiah by bearing our infirmities, He is the friend of sinners whose new wine bursts the old forms, and He is the Shepherd moved with compassion for the lost. One response, faith that simply comes to Him, is commended again and again in the leper, the centurion and the bleeding woman. The other, the Gadarene town begging Him to leave because they preferred their pigs, stands as a warning.

Jesus called His twelve disciples and gave them His own authority over unclean spirits and power to heal every kind of sickness. Their first commission was narrow: to go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel rather than to the Gentiles or Samaritans. Their message was the same one John and Jesus preached, 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand.' They were to give freely as they had received, taking no gold or extra provisions, depending entirely on the One who sent them.

Jesus warned that He was sending them as sheep among wolves; they would be handed over to councils, dragged before governors, and hated for His name, though whoever endures to the end will be saved. He told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. Yet three times He said 'Do not fear.' They should not fear those who can kill the body but not the soul, because not even a sparrow falls without the Father's will, the hairs of their heads are numbered, and they are worth more than many sparrows.

The first mark is confession: owning Christ openly before people, since He will confess before the Father those who confess Him and deny those who deny Him. The second is a love for Him that outranks every rival, even father and mother; following Him may bring a sword and division within a household. The third is taking up the cross and following Him, losing one's life for His sake in order to find true life. The lesson sums it up as seeing Him clearly, loving Him dearly and following Him nearly, also described as commitment, confession and cost, like a brand that shows whose we are.

Sitting in Herod's prison, John began to doubt and sent his disciples to ask, 'Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?' Jesus did not rebuke this honest question.
