He pointed to His works: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor hear the gospel, the signs Isaiah had promised of the kingdom. He added, 'Blessed is he who is not offended because of Me,' and then honored John publicly as the greatest born of women, though the least in the kingdom is greater.

The invitation is addressed to all who labor and are heavy laden, the weary and burdened. It comes right after Jesus pronounced woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum for refusing to repent, so the King who warns the hard-hearted opens His arms to the tired. He offers rest for their souls and invites them to take His yoke and learn from Him, because He is gentle and lowly in heart. His yoke is easy and His burden light; His rule is not another load but true rest.

When the hungry disciples plucked grain on the Sabbath, the Pharisees objected, but Jesus answered from Scripture: David ate the showbread and the priests work in the temple. He quoted 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' and claimed that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. Then He healed a man with a withered hand in the synagogue, arguing that if they would rescue a sheep from a pit, it is lawful to do good to a man on the Sabbath. The Pharisees had buried the Sabbath under rules, and Jesus restored it as a gift for people's good, but they went out and plotted to destroy Him.

When Jesus cast a demon out of a blind and mute man, the Pharisees could not deny the miracle, so they claimed He cast out demons by Beelzebub, the ruler of demons. Jesus exposed the folly of this: a kingdom or house divided against itself cannot stand, so Satan would not cast out Satan. If instead He casts out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon them. He drew the line clearly: whoever is not with Him is against Him, and He warned about blasphemy against the Spirit.

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is not a single careless word but the settled, willful and final rejection of the Spirit's witness to Christ, as when the Pharisees looked at the Spirit's own work and knowingly called it the devil's. It is unbelief carried to the point of no return. It cannot be forgiven not because God's grace runs out, but because the person who persists in calling good evil has shut the only door through which forgiveness comes. The lesson adds comfort: someone who fears having committed it still has a tender conscience, a sign the Spirit is still at work.

When the scribes and Pharisees demanded a sign, Jesus refused to perform a miracle on command for an evil and adulterous generation. Instead He promised only the sign of the prophet Jonah: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, the Son of Man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. This points to His death and resurrection, the one sign that settles everything. He added that the men of Nineveh who repented at Jonah's preaching will condemn this generation, because one greater than Jonah is here.

When His mother and brothers came looking for Him, Jesus pointed to His disciples and said that whoever does the will of His Father in heaven is His brother, sister and mother. His true family is bound not by blood but by obedience to the Father. This gathers the unit's two tracks: the mission goes out and forms a new people around the King, while opposition rises from Pharisees and unrepentant cities. Since 'he who is not with Me is against Me,' there is no neutral ground, and each person must decide whether to be with Him by doing the Father's will.

A parable is an earthly story that carries a heavenly meaning, and it both reveals and conceals. When the disciples asked why He used them, Jesus said it had been given to them to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but not to the others. To the hungry heart that wants to understand, the story opens the truth; to the hardened heart that has already turned away, it stays a riddle, fulfilling Isaiah's words, 'Seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear.' The parables describe a hidden kingdom that grows quietly in this age.

A sower scatters seed, which Jesus explains is the word of the kingdom, on four kinds of ground. Seed on the wayside path is snatched away by the evil one before it takes root. Seed on rocky ground springs up quickly but withers under trouble and persecution because it has no root. Seed among thorns is choked by the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches. Seed on good ground bears fruit, a hundred, sixty or thirtyfold. The seed is the same; the difference is the soil of the heart.

A man sowed good seed, but while people slept an enemy sowed tares, darnel, which looks so much like wheat that the two cannot be safely told apart until harvest. The master forbade the servants to pull the weeds, lest they uproot the wheat, and said to let both grow until harvest. Jesus explains that the field is the world, the good seed the sons of the kingdom, the tares the sons of the wicked one, the enemy the devil, the harvest the end of the age, and the reapers the angels. The main lesson is that the kingdom grows in a mixed field, and the final separation belongs to God at the end, not to us now; we should exercise discernment but focus on sowing good seed and making sure our own faith is genuine.

The mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, grows into a tree large enough for birds to nest in, and a little leaven hidden in three measures of meal works through until the whole is leavened. Both show that the kingdom starts small and nearly invisible, like a few fishermen and a teacher in a borrowed boat, yet grows until it spreads through everything. The King builds His kingdom not by force or spectacle but by quiet, sure growth. So we must not despise small and hidden beginnings.

A man found treasure hidden in a field and, for joy, sold all he had to buy that field; a merchant searching for fine pearls found one of great price and sold everything to buy it. The two parables make one point from two directions: one man stumbles on the kingdom by surprise, the other seeks and finds. Both teach that the kingdom of heaven is worth everything. Giving all for it is not a grim sacrifice but a glad exchange made for joy, the best bargain anyone could make.

The kingdom is like a dragnet let down into the sea that gathers fish of every kind; when it is full, the fishermen sort the good from the bad. Jesus says that at the end of the age the angels will separate the wicked from among the just. Like the wheat and tares, it teaches that there is a mixture of good and bad now, in the world and even in the visible church. Both parables stress that the final separation is certain and that it is God's work at the end, not ours now.

After the disciples say they understand, Jesus compares every scribe instructed in the kingdom to a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old. The disciple who understands the kingdom is like a steward with a full storehouse, able to bring out the old treasure of the Scriptures and the new treasure of their fulfillment in Christ. The new does not discard the old but opens it up. That is exactly what Matthew does throughout his Gospel, showing how the King's new work fulfills the old promises.

Jesus returned to His hometown of Nazareth and taught in the synagogue, and the people were astonished at His wisdom, but they took offense, saying He was only the carpenter's son whose family they knew. Jesus said a prophet is not without honor except in his own country and house, and He did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief. This is the parable of the soils come to life: the same word that bears fruit in good soil was snatched from hard hearts. Familiarity made them think they already knew Him, so the seed found no root.

Together the parables show that in this age the kingdom does not come in overwhelming glory but is sown like seed that roots in some hearts and not in others. It grows in a mixed field of wheat and tares, to be separated by God, not by us, at the end. It starts small and hidden like the mustard seed and leaven, yet spreads through the whole. It is hidden like treasure, yet worth everything. And it moves toward a final harvest when the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom.

The one response the chapter calls for is a heart that hears the word, understands it and bears fruit, the good soil of Matthew 13:23. Each hearer should ask which soil he is, since the parables are meant to search our hearts now rather than satisfy curiosity about the future. A kingdom that grows like seed calls for patience, a mixed field calls for humility since we cannot finally judge another's heart, and a kingdom worth everything calls for giving all we have. To know its mysteries is finally to give ourselves to the King.

After feeding the five thousand, Jesus sent the disciples ahead in the boat and came to them walking on the water. Peter asked to come, stepped out and walked on the waves for a moment, but when he saw the wind he became afraid, began to sink and cried, 'Lord, save me!' Jesus caught him and asked why he doubted, calling him 'you of little faith.' When Jesus entered the boat and the wind stopped, the disciples worshiped Him as truly the Son of God. It reveals Jesus' divine authority over the sea and shows that Peter's faith was real but wavered when he looked at the storm instead of Christ.

The Pharisees were upset that the disciples ate without the ceremonial hand-washing of their tradition. Jesus answered that what goes into the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the mouth does. The reason is that it comes from the heart, and out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries and other sins. So defilement is a matter of the heart, not of outward ceremony.

A Gentile woman from Canaan begged Jesus to heal her daughter, who was tormented by a demon. At first Jesus seemed to refuse her, testing her, but she kept pressing with humble persistence. Jesus marveled and said, 'O woman, great is your faith! Let it be to you as you desire,' and her daughter was healed. Like the centurion earlier, an outsider shows the faith the King is looking for, a sign that His church will gather people from every nation.

At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asked who people said He was, and they answered John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah or one of the prophets. Then He asked, 'But who do you say that I am?' Peter answered, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' Jesus called him blessed because flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but the Father in heaven. So the confession did not come from Peter's own cleverness or from hearsay; it was revealed by God.

The lesson notes a play on words: Peter's name (Petros) means a small stone, while the rock (petra) on which the church is built is the bedrock truth Peter just confessed by the Spirit's revelation, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. So the church is built not on a man but on Christ confessed, and Christ Himself builds it. Gates are defensive, so the promise that the gates of Hades will not prevail means the church is meant to advance and hell's defenses will not hold against it. The King also gives His people the keys of the kingdom to open its doors through the gospel.

Right after the confession, Jesus began to show the disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed and be raised on the third day. When Peter rebuked Him, Jesus said, 'Get behind Me, Satan,' because Peter was thinking of human things, not God's. He then taught that anyone who wants to follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross and follow Him, for whoever saves his life will lose it and whoever loses it for His sake will find it. Self-denial means giving up the throne of self, like handing Christ the keys to every room; the cross is suffering that comes from doing God's will; and following means walking in His steps rather than asking Him to bless our own path.

Six days later Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain and was transfigured before them, His face shining like the sun. Moses and Elijah, representing the law and the prophets, appeared and talked with Him, and Peter offered to build three tabernacles. Then a bright cloud overshadowed them, and the Father repeated what He said at the Jordan, adding a command: 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear Him!' The glory confirms Peter's confession and shows that Jesus, not Moses or Elijah, is the one to be heard.

When the disciples asked who is greatest in the kingdom, Jesus set a little child among them and said that unless they are converted and become like little children they will not enter the kingdom. True greatness is the humility of a child, not rank. He warned that causing one of these little ones to stumble is so serious that a millstone around the neck and drowning would be better. And through the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one stray, He showed it is not the Father's will that any little one perish, so the church must guard and seek its weakest members.

If a brother sins against you, first go to him privately and tell him his fault. If he will not listen, take one or two others with you, and if he still refuses, tell it to the church. The goal at each step is to win the brother back, not to expose him, and the church is given real authority to bind and loose, exercising loving discipline. In that setting Jesus promised that where two or three are gathered in His name, He is there in the midst of them, so the King is present even in a small gathering.

When Peter asked whether forgiving seven times was enough, Jesus said seventy times seven, meaning without keeping count. In the parable a king forgave a servant an unpayable debt, but that servant then seized a fellow servant over a trifling sum and had him jailed; the king handed the wicked servant to the tormentors, and Jesus warned the Father will do the same to those who do not forgive from the heart. This gathers the unit's theme because the church built on the confession of Christ is a community of the forgiven. Its life should look like its King: humble, caring for the weak, correcting in love, and forgiving without limit because it has been forgiven so much.

When the Pharisees tested Him on divorce, Jesus pointed back to creation: what God has joined together, let no man separate. When the disciples pushed children away, He welcomed them, saying the kingdom belongs to such as these. When the rich young man asked what good deed to do, Jesus told him to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow Him, and he went away sad because he was very rich. Jesus said this is impossible with men but possible with God. These teachings show the kingdom cannot be bought or earned but only received like a child, by God's grace.

A landowner hired workers at dawn and then again at the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours, and at the end of the day he paid them all the same wage. Those hired first complained, but he said he had done them no wrong, since he paid what was agreed, and he was free to be generous to the others. Jesus concluded that the last will be first and the first last. The kingdom runs not on the arithmetic of wages but on God's generosity: no one earns a place, and the latecomer receives the same grace as the one who worked all day.

Right after Jesus foretold His death a third time, the mother of James and John asked for her sons to sit at His right and left, and the other ten were indignant. Jesus overturned the world's idea of greatness: whoever wants to be great must be the servant of others, and whoever wants to be first must be a slave. He pointed to Himself, saying the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. Greatness in His kingdom is measured by service, not by thrones.

Jesus sent for a donkey and rode into Jerusalem, deliberately fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy that the King would come lowly, riding on a donkey. The crowds spread garments and branches and shouted, 'Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the LORD!' He entered as the rightful King, but in peace and humility rather than on a war horse, the opposite of the conquering deliverer many expected. He then went to the temple and drove out the money changers, claiming His Father's house as a house of prayer.

An owner rented his vineyard to tenants, and when he sent servants to collect the fruit, the tenants beat and killed them; finally he sent his son, and they killed him to seize the vineyard. Jesus applied it with Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. He warned the leaders that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to a people that bears its fruit, and they knew He meant them. The lesson's sermon adds that the tenants' great sin was acting as if the vineyard were theirs; it is a lesson in stewardship, asking what we are doing with what belongs to God.

When the Pharisees tried to trap Him about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus answered, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's,' giving both their due and escaping the trap. When the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, mocked it with a riddle, He corrected them, saying God is not the God of the dead but of the living. In both cases He silenced His opponents with perfect wisdom.

When a lawyer asked which is the great commandment, Jesus said to love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and that the second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. He said that on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. So the whole law is summed up in love for God and love for neighbor, and every other command depends on them.

In a series of woes Jesus condemned the scribes and Pharisees because they said and did not do, loaded heavy burdens on others, and loved the best seats and titles. He called them blind guides who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel, and who clean the outside of the cup while the inside is full of greed. He compared them to whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside but full of dead men's bones. The deepest sin He named was hypocrisy, a religion of appearances with a dead heart.

After all the conflict, Jesus cried, 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the one who kills the prophets,' saying how often He wanted to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they were not willing, so their house would be left desolate. This is not the anger of a tyrant but the sorrow of a Savior. It reveals a heart of tender love and longing for the very people who were rejecting Him and would crucify Him.

The road to Jerusalem shows the King coming to His own: He enters His city as rightful King but humbly on a donkey, cleanses His Father's house, and answers every challenge with wisdom. He redefines greatness as service and the whole law as love for God and neighbor, and He exposes the leaders' hollow religion, warning that the kingdom will go to those who bear fruit. Throughout He walks deliberately toward the cross, since the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many. He went up on purpose, knowing what awaited Him, and loving the very city that would crucify Him.

As Jesus and the disciples were leaving the temple, He said that not one stone would be left on another. Later, sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came with three questions: when will the temple be destroyed, what will be the sign of Your coming, and what will be the sign of the end of the age? Jesus answered all three, but the answers are woven so closely that interpreters still debate which verses answer which question. The discourse was given less to satisfy curiosity than to make His people ready, so we should hold it with humility.

About forty years after the prediction, in A.D. 70, Roman legions under Titus surrounded Jerusalem and cut off its supplies. Inside, people died from famine, civil war between factions and disease; Josephus describes people eating shoe leather and even cannibalism. The temple was burned, its gold melted, and soldiers pried the stones apart to recover the gold, literally leaving not one stone on another. Hundreds of thousands died and many were enslaved, and for first-century Jews it was the end of their world: the priesthood and sacrifices ceased, leaving only part of the western retaining wall.

Jesus described false christs deceiving many, wars and rumors of wars, famines and earthquakes, which are only the beginning of sorrows, not the end. His people would be hated and persecuted, yet the gospel of the kingdom would be preached to all nations before the end comes. He spoke of the abomination of desolation, a great tribulation, and the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and glory to gather His elect. Interpreters disagree over how much of this pointed to A.D. 70 and how much reaches forward to His final coming, but all agree on the fig tree's lesson and that His words will not pass away.

Jesus said plainly that no one knows the day or hour of His return, not even the Son, but only the Father. Even so, people have predicted dates for two thousand years, and every prediction has failed; by the test of Deuteronomy 18, a prophet whose prediction fails is a false prophet. Harold Camping used homemade numerology to set May 21, 2011, and then moved it to October when nothing happened. His followers drained savings, abandoned careers and suffered spiritual disillusionment, showing that claiming divine authority for human calculations not only fails but wounds those who trust it.

In the parable of the ten virgins, five had oil for their lamps and five did not, and when the bridegroom came the door was shut on those who were unprepared. The point is that we must be ready at all times, because we do not know the hour of His coming and readiness cannot be borrowed at the last minute. The image of one taken and one left makes the same point: people living side by side in ordinary life will be separated suddenly when He comes. So the call is to watch and stay prepared.

Premillennialism holds that Christ returns before a literal future thousand-year reign on earth; it comes in historic and dispensational forms and was held by Justin Martyr and Irenaeus. Postmillennialism expects Christ to return after a long golden age in which the gospel gradually wins the nations, as Jonathan Edwards and the Puritans held. Amillennialism sees the thousand years as symbolic of Christ's present reign from heaven between His two comings, the view of Augustine, Luther and Calvin. The unit treats them even-handedly: sincere Bible-loving believers have held each for centuries, none is a test of fellowship, and all agree on Christ's bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgment.

The first time Jesus came as the suffering Servant of Isaiah, born in a stable, rejected and crucified between thieves; when He comes again He will come as a conquering King. First Thessalonians 4 gives the clearest picture: at the sound of the trumpet the dead in Christ will rise first, and then those who are alive will be caught up to join them. Paul wrote this to comfort believers anxious about loved ones who had died, assuring them death is no barrier. The trumpet, like the shofar, signals God's presence, liberation and coronation all at once.

The unit rejects 'soul sleep,' the idea that the soul is unconscious between death and resurrection. Jesus told the thief he would be with Him in Paradise that very day, and Paul says to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. The 'sleep' Scripture speaks of refers to the body resting in the grave, while the soul remains awake and with God. Dr. Cook's mailbox illustration makes the point: the body is only the mailbox, but the letter, the real person, is already safe in the sender's hands until the day of delivery.

Believers will receive glorified bodies like Jesus' resurrection body, which passed through locked doors, could be recognized or not, ate fish, and ascended into a cloud. Even greater, 1 John 3:2 says that when He appears we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. In the Old Testament no one could look on God's face, and Moses saw only His back, but we will see Him face to face because we will have been made like Him. The mystery is that God will make us holy without erasing who we are, keeping our identity, memory and freedom while purifying us.

The discourse moves from what we cannot know, the date, through what we are promised, the events of that day, to what we can barely imagine, what we shall become: from humility, through hope, to wonder. Chapter 25 then turns this into an urgent call. The ten virgins teach readiness, the talents teach faithfulness with what we have been given so we may hear 'Well done,' and the sheep and goats show the King judging by what was done to the least of His brethren. So the call is to watch, be faithful and love, because the King will surely come.

The chief priests plotted to arrest Jesus by trickery and kill Him. Meanwhile at Bethany a woman poured costly fragrant oil on His head; the disciples called it a waste, but Jesus defended her, saying she had done a good work and prepared His body for burial, showing He knew where His road led. In contrast, Judas went to the chief priests and agreed to betray Him for thirty pieces of silver. The same moment brought out both the deepest devotion and the darkest treachery.

At the Passover meal Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and said, 'Take, eat; this is My body.' Then He took the cup and said, 'Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.' This means the old Passover, which remembered the lamb whose blood spared Israel in Egypt, gives way to the new covenant in the blood of Jesus, the true Lamb. The Lord's Supper is not a funeral but a remembrance and a promise, looking back to the cross and forward to drinking it new with Him in the Father's kingdom.

In the garden Jesus told Peter, James and John that His soul was sorrowful to the point of death, then fell on His face and prayed, 'O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.' He prayed this three times and three times found the disciples asleep, warning them to watch and pray because the spirit is willing but the flesh weak. His prayer shows that the real cost of the cross began not with the nails but with surrendering His will to the Father's. He shrank from the cup yet freely took it for us.

While Jesus was still speaking, Judas arrived with a crowd armed with swords and clubs and betrayed Him with a kiss. When one of His followers drew a sword and struck, Jesus told him to put it away, because all who take the sword will perish by the sword. He said He could call more than twelve legions of angels, but then the Scriptures would not be fulfilled, so He went willingly. Then all the disciples forsook Him and fled, leaving Him to face trial alone.

Jesus was taken to Caiaphas the high priest, where they looked for false witnesses whose testimony did not agree. Finally the high priest put Him under oath and demanded to know if He was the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus answered, 'It is as you said,' and spoke of the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his clothes and called it blasphemy, and the council condemned Him as deserving death, then spat on Him and struck Him.

Peter had sworn he would die rather than deny Jesus, but in the high priest's courtyard, questioned by a servant girl and others, he denied knowing Him three times. When the rooster crowed, he remembered the Lord's words and went out and wept bitterly. It shows that even the boldest disciple discovered his own weakness in the very hour his Master was condemned. Self-confidence fails, and our loyalty is weaker than we think.

Pilate, the Roman governor, found no fault in Jesus but feared the crowd. Following a feast custom, he offered to release either Jesus or Barabbas, a notorious criminal, expecting them to choose Jesus. Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd demanded Barabbas and shouted for Jesus to be crucified; Pilate washed his hands and the people said, 'His blood be on us and on our children.' The guilty man went free while the innocent King was condemned in his place, a picture of substitution, of what the cross itself would do for sinners.

The soldiers mocked Jesus with a scarlet robe and crown of thorns, Simon of Cyrene carried His cross to Golgotha, and He was crucified between two robbers under the charge 'This is Jesus the King of the Jews,' while the priests mocked that He saved others but could not save Himself. From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covered the land, and He cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' That cry shows the sinless Son bearing others' sins and the separation sin brings, yet it opens Psalm 22, which moves toward victory. Then He cried out again and yielded up His spirit, the veil tore from top to bottom, and the earth quaked.

The veil tore from top to bottom, showing God Himself opened the way. First came down the curtain of separation: the temple's graded courts divided high priest, priests, Israelite men, women and Gentiles, but in Christ all are one. Second, the curtain of mediation: once only the high priest could enter God's presence, but now there is one Mediator, Christ Jesus, and every believer is a priest with direct access to God. Third, the curtain of sin, which we built and could not remove; Christ tore it from His side by His body and blood, opening a new and living way, though His blood must be applied by receiving Him as Lord and Savior.

Seeing the earthquake and everything that happened, the centurion and the guards were terrified and said, 'Truly this was the Son of God!', a Roman confessing what the religious leaders would not. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asked Pilate for the body, wrapped it in clean linen and laid it in his own new tomb with a great stone; the chief priests had the tomb sealed and guarded, unknowingly providing witnesses to the resurrection. The Passion sums up the Gospel because the King who came to give His life as a ransom now gives it; because He would not save Himself, He can save all who receive Him.

At dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. There was a great earthquake as an angel of the Lord came down, rolled back the stone and sat on it, shining like lightning, and the guards shook and became like dead men. The angel told the women not to be afraid: 'He is not here; for He is risen, as He said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.' The stone was rolled away not to let Jesus out, since He had already risen, but to let the witnesses in.

The women hurried from the tomb with fear and great joy to tell the disciples, and on the way Jesus Himself met them and said, 'Rejoice!' They held His feet and worshiped Him, and He told them to tell His brothers to go to Galilee, where they would see Him. Over the next forty days He appeared again and again. Paul records that on one occasion more than five hundred people saw Him at once, many still living and available to be questioned. The lesson calls the resurrection the best-attested event of the ancient world, not a fable.

Some of the guards went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened. The leaders met and paid the soldiers a large sum to say that the disciples came by night and stole the body while they slept, and that story spread. But the lie actually testifies to the resurrection, because Jesus' enemies did not deny the tomb was empty and could not produce a body. They could only invent a weak story, since sleeping men cannot testify to a theft they slept through.

The women came to the tomb in grief, carrying spices for a final service, and left running with great joy, because the resurrection answers our deepest distress, death itself. Dr. Cook tells how his baby niece, born with fluid on the brain, died after an operation when he was about fourteen, and his mother cried, 'Why did God let our baby die?' He admits he still has no full answer to that question. But he believes he will see her again because the tomb is empty and Christ is risen. The resurrection does not pretend the grave is nothing, but it promises the grave is not the end.

Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared to the disciples, and he refused to believe unless he saw the nail scars and touched them, because he knew dead men do not rise. A week later Jesus appeared again with Thomas present and showed him His hands and side, and Thomas cried, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus did not rebuke him for needing to see but met him in his doubt and turned it into worship. Dr. Cook admits his own doubts about God, the faith, prayer and his calling, and says the resurrection conquers them: if Christ is risen, God is real, the gospel is true and death is defeated.

Peter had sworn he would never fall away, yet he denied Jesus three times, the last time with cursing. The risen Lord did not leave him in his guilt; on the seashore He asked him three times, 'Do you love Me?', one question for each denial, and three times restored his calling with 'Feed My sheep.' The same Peter who denied Christ in a courtyard preached Him boldly on the day of Pentecost. Dr. Cook confesses he has denied Christ through silence, and the resurrection answers that too: the Lord who restored Peter restores us, and the Spirit can make us bold to speak.

Saul of Tarsus was full of hatred for the church, going house to house dragging believers off to prison. On the road to Damascus a light from heaven flashed around him, he fell, and a voice said, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?'; when he asked who it was, he heard, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' Meeting the risen Christ transformed him so completely that the great persecutor became the great missionary. The resurrection can break even a heart set in hatred or bitterness and turn disgust into worship.

On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus said, 'All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.' Based on His authority, it commands us to go to all nations and make disciples, not just converts, baptized in the triune name and taught to obey everything He commanded. It is the marching order of the whole church, making demands on our lips (the message), our feet ('Go'), our heads (the vision of all nations) and our hearts (the burden to go or send).

Matthew begins by saying the child will be called Immanuel, 'God with us' (1:23), and ends with the risen Lord promising, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age' (28:20). The whole Gospel is held between these two statements. The God who came to be with us in the manger, through the teaching and miracles and even into the darkness of the cross, is now with us as the risen, reigning King. He will remain with His people every day until the age ends, so the Immanuel of the beginning still walks with us.

The resurrection proves Jesus is alive and defeats our distress over death, our doubt, our denial and our disgust or hatred, as seen in the grieving women, Thomas, Peter and Saul. Every other grave has footsteps leading in, but Jesus' grave has footsteps leading out, and because He lives all who are in Christ will live too. Our response is to be His witnesses and obey the Great Commission: go under the authority of the living King and make disciples of all nations. We go confident that He is with us always, to the end of the age.

Romans was written by the Apostle Paul, born Saul in Tarsus around AD 5 to Jewish parents who held Roman citizenship. As a teenager he studied in Jerusalem under Rabbi Gamaliel, the most respected teacher in Israel, but unlike his moderate mentor he was a fierce persecutor of the church. He approved of Stephen's stoning and went house to house dragging believers to prison, sincerely convinced he was serving God. Everything changed when the risen Jesus confronted him on the Damascus road.

Paul wrote Romans in the late winter or early spring of AD 57 from Corinth, near the end of his third missionary journey. He was about to take a relief offering to the poor believers in Jerusalem and then hoped to visit Rome and go on to Spain. The letter was carried to Rome by Phoebe, a deaconess of the church at Cenchrea, whom Paul commends in chapter 16. She was entrusted with delivering it and reading it in the Roman house churches.

Romans 1:17 says the righteousness of God is revealed in the gospel "from faith to faith," quoting Habakkuk 2:4: "The just shall live by faith." It sets out three claims the whole letter develops: righteousness, being right with God, comes from God rather than our own effort; it is received by faith from start to finish; and the result is life with God, not merely escape from condemnation. The rest of Romans explains how a sinful person can be made right with a holy God, which is exactly what this verse announces.

Martin Luther was a German monk who had done everything religion demanded, including vows, fasting, long prayers, a doctorate in theology, and climbing Pilate's stairs in Rome on his knees, yet he remained terrified of God. While teaching Romans to his students at Wittenberg, he meditated on "The just shall live by faith." He came to see that salvation is not earned by discipline but is a gift received by trusting Christ. That discovery freed him and sparked the Protestant Reformation.

On May 24, 1738, John Wesley, a discouraged Anglican missionary who had failed for two years in Georgia, went unwillingly to a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. Someone read aloud Luther's preface to his commentary on Romans, and around a quarter to nine Wesley felt his heart "strangely warmed." He trusted in Christ alone for salvation and received assurance that his sins were taken away. The same message of Romans that had transformed Luther now transformed Wesley, and from that night came the Wesleyan Revival and eventually the Methodist Church.

The Roman church was not founded by Paul, and he had never visited it. It probably began with Jews who believed at Pentecost (Acts 2) and brought the gospel home to Rome. By Paul's time it was a network of small house churches scattered around the capital, made up of both Jewish and Gentile believers. These fellowships were known throughout the world for the strength of their faith.

The Greek word doulos means more than an employee or follower; it describes a slave who has been purchased outright and owns nothing apart from what his master allows. By opening with this title, Paul identifies himself first as the legal property of Jesus Christ. It expresses total ownership, submission, and devotion to his Master. Paul also says he was separated, or set apart, to the gospel, meaning he did not volunteer but was claimed for God's purpose.

Romans 1:16 says the gospel is the power of God to salvation. Paul is not ashamed of it because it actually accomplishes what it announces: it saves. It is offered to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek, meaning Gentiles. Faith, not ethnicity or law-keeping, is the condition for receiving it.

Romans is so influential because it lays out the gospel line by line in one sustained argument, answering how a sinful person can be right with a holy God. It does not assume faith or start with tips for living; it faces the bad news honestly and then presents the good news fully. Across the centuries God has used it to convert Augustine, to bring Luther to the truth that sparked the Reformation, and to warm Wesley's heart and ignite revival. Understanding Romans means understanding the heart of Christianity.

In Romans 1:18-3:20 Paul proves that the whole human race is guilty before God before he announces the remedy. He shows first that pagan Gentiles suppress the truth, ignore God's revelation in creation, and turn to idols, so God gives them over to their sin. Then he shows that the moral person who judges others and the religious Jew who has the law are equally guilty, because they do the same things and outward credentials cannot save. He closes with a chain of Old Testament quotations declaring that none is righteous, so every mouth is stopped and all the world stands guilty, since no one is justified by works of the law.

First, people suppress the truth in wickedness; the truth is not hidden, but they hold it down because their sin drives them to avoid God. Second, they ignore God's general revelation in creation, where His eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen, so they are without excuse. Third, they exchange the glory of the immortal God for images of humans, birds, animals, and reptiles. Paul presents these as three downward steps every fallen person takes, and they show that God's judgment is just.

Three times Paul says "God gave them over": first to sexual impurity and the degrading of their bodies, then to shameful or vile passions that disorder natural sexual function, and finally to a debased mind that can no longer tell good from evil and even approves of evil. The sequence descends deeper each time. It teaches that God's wrath is not always fire from heaven; often it is God withdrawing His restraint and letting people have what they keep demanding. The resulting list of sins, from murder to gossip to disobeying parents, is all called wickedness, with no ranking that lets us feel better than others.

Paul turns to the reader who agrees that pagans are terrible and says he has no excuse, because in judging others he condemns himself by doing the same things. By judging, he proves he knows God's standard, and by failing it he stands condemned by his own verdict. Paul then gives four principles of God's judgment: it is according to truth, without partiality, according to works, and it reaches the secrets of the heart through Christ. Even the conscience of Gentiles bears witness against them, since everyone fails the standard their own conscience admits.

Paul lists the Jewish reader's credentials: he bears the name Jew, relies on the law, boasts in God, and knows His will. Then he asks whether the one who teaches others teaches himself, whether the one who preaches against stealing and adultery does those very things. Having the law without obeying it does not protect anyone; it actually deepens guilt. Paul concludes that true Jewishness is inward, not outward, so religious privilege and external signs like circumcision cannot save.

Circumcision was the covenant sign and the deepest mark of Jewish identity, but Paul says the outward mark means nothing without the inward reality. Circumcision of the heart is an inner work done by the Spirit, not by the letter of the law, that truly changes a person. This is what God has always required. The principle also applies to Christians: baptism, church attendance, or denominational membership cannot replace a transformed heart.

Paul states that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, and he proves it with a chain of Old Testament quotations from the Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah: none is righteous, none understands, none seeks God, none does good. These quotations fall like a judge's gavel, describing sin in the throat, lips, mouth, feet, and eyes. The law speaks so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become guilty before God. No one has a defense left, and no one can be justified by works of the law.

Romans 3:20 says that no one will be justified by the works of the law, because through the law comes the knowledge of sin. The law was never given to save anyone. It was given to expose the disease that requires salvation, showing people God's perfect standard and how far short they fall. In that way it stops every mouth and prepares us to look for God's righteousness by faith.

Paul wants people to understand the disease before he offers the cure. Like a doctor who must explain the illness before the patient will take the medicine, he closes every escape route so readers see that they truly need rescue. The gospel is not vague comfort but specific rescue from a specific disaster, and it only makes sense to someone who knows they are lost. Once every mouth is stopped, the "But now" of Romans 3:21 shines all the brighter.

James 2:10 says that whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point is guilty of all, so even a single failure breaks the law. In Matthew 5:48 Jesus raised the bar further by commanding, "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." Together they show that God's standard is not relative goodness or doing better than others but absolute righteousness. Since everyone falls short of that perfect standard, no one can be justified by keeping the law, which supports Paul's conclusion that all have sinned.

Romans 3:21 begins with "But now," turning from sixty-six verses of indictment to the announcement of rescue. Up to this point Paul has acted like a prosecutor, proving that the openly wicked, the moralist, and the religious insider are all guilty and every mouth is stopped. Now he declares that God has revealed a righteousness apart from the law, witnessed by the Law and the Prophets, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. The book moves from bad news to good news here, which is why Luther saw this passage as the chief place of the whole letter.

Justification is a legal, courtroom term. It does not mean being made morally perfect but being declared righteous, pronounced not guilty before God. It is a verdict, not a gradual process: God announces that the believer's debt is paid in full and he is acquitted. This righteousness is not our own but is credited to us from outside ourselves, what Luther called alien righteousness. Paul says we are justified freely by God's grace, through faith, apart from the works of the law.

Propitiation is a temple word. The Greek hilasterion refers to the mercy seat, the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant where the high priest sprinkled the blood of atonement on the Day of Atonement. Paul says God set forth Christ as that mercy seat. God's wrath against sin was real and His justice required satisfaction, so on the cross that wrath fell on Christ and the believing sinner goes free.

Grace is the source: God's unearned favor, which justifies us freely (dorean), as a gift and without any cause in us. Redemption is the means: like a slave bought out of bondage, we were purchased from slavery to sin at the price of Christ's blood. Faith is how we receive it: Christ's propitiating sacrifice is applied to those who believe. God gives, Christ pays, and the sinner simply trusts, so the whole transaction runs in one direction, from God to us.

Abraham was the central figure of Jewish faith, the father of the nation, and the recipient of the covenant, the prime example of a righteous man. If even Abraham was justified by faith rather than works, then justification has always been by faith. Paul shows from Genesis 15:6 that Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, long before the law or circumcision. That makes Abraham the father of all who believe, Jews and Gentiles alike.

Genesis 15:6 says, "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness." Paul builds his whole argument on this verse, which was written before the law of Moses, circumcision, or the sacrificial system. The word "accounted" (logizomai) is a bookkeeping term meaning to credit to an account. God did not find righteousness in Abraham; He credited it to a man who had none, on the basis of faith.

Abraham was credited with righteousness in Genesis 15, but circumcision was not instituted until Genesis 17, many years later. So Abraham was justified by faith while he was still uncircumcised. Circumcision came afterward as a sign confirming a righteousness he already had by faith, not as the cause of it. The order is faith first, then the sign, then works, which shows that no religious act earns justification and makes Abraham the father of uncircumcised Gentile believers too.

To credit or impute righteousness is a bookkeeping idea (logizomai): God puts righteousness on the believer's account even though the believer did not produce it. It is not wages earned, which would be a debt God owes, but a gift of grace to someone who does not work but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly. The righteousness comes from outside us, from God through Christ. The same righteousness God credited to Abraham He credits to everyone who believes in the One who raised Jesus from the dead.

Romans 4:25 says Jesus "was delivered up because of our offenses, and was raised because of our justification." His death on the cross paid the penalty for our sins. His resurrection was the Father's vindication, showing that the payment was accepted, like God's "amen" to the cross. In one sentence the verse joins the cross and the empty tomb as the basis of our being declared righteous.

If justification depended on our performance, we could never be sure we had done enough, and any boasting would rest on ourselves. Because it rests on what Christ has done and is received by faith alone, it is a finished verdict: God declares the believer righteous and says the debt is paid in full. God's justice is satisfied in the cross, so He is both just and the justifier, and the resurrection proves the payment was accepted. Our confidence therefore rests on Christ's work and God's promise, not on our own changing record.

Because we have been justified by faith, a finished verdict, Paul names three benefits. First, we have peace with God through Christ; this is not mainly a feeling but a legal fact that the war between holy God and sinful people is over. Second, we have access by faith into the grace in which we stand, an ongoing entry into God's presence, not a one-time visit. Third, we rejoice in hope of the glory of God, which is a confident expectation of a guaranteed future rather than wishful thinking.

Paul says believers rejoice in tribulations because suffering sets off a chain. Tribulation produces perseverance, the ability to endure under pressure. Perseverance produces character, a proven worth like metal tested in fire and found genuine. Character produces hope, which is surprising because the world expects suffering to kill hope, but each hardship faithfully endured deepens our assurance that God is at work and His promises are real.

Hope does not disappoint because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who was given to us. The Christian's confidence does not depend on circumstances staying favorable. It rests on God's love, already proven at the cross and already certified by the Spirit living inside the believer. Because that love is already given, the hope it supports cannot put us to shame.

Paul uses four words for our condition when Christ died for us. We were powerless, unable to produce any righteousness for ourselves. We were ungodly, not just weak but turned against God. We were sinners, actively rebelling. And in verse 10 we were enemies, at war with the very God who came to rescue us. The list rises in intensity and shows that Christ's love reached us at our worst.

Romans 5:8 says God shows His love in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Human love, even the best, like a sacrificial mother or a faithful wife, usually goes to people who are close to us or love us back. God's love came before we cleaned ourselves up, before we sought Him, and even before we knew our need. Jesus did not just give His life to us but gave it for us, a love no other religion offers and no human heart could invent.

Romans 5:12 teaches that sin entered the world through one man, Adam, and death through sin, so death spread to all people. This is called original sin. Adam did not sin only as an individual but as the federal head, the representative, of the human race, so his guilt was imputed to all his descendants, much as a head of state's act binds a nation. This is the first imputation in the Bible and the counterpart to the imputation of Christ's righteousness.

The framework compares the first and second Adam on three levels. Core: by birth Adam gives us a sinful nature, but by new birth Christ gives a spiritual nature. Consequences: Adam brings death, while Christ brings life, so that believers even reign in life through Him. Condition: Adam produces guilt before God, while Christ produces forgiveness and justification, through the same principle of representation and imputation.

A type is a real historical person whose story is a divinely intended pattern that prefigures a greater fulfillment in Christ. Adam is a type because, like Christ, he stood as the representative head of a humanity, and what he did affected everyone under him. Adam's one act brought sin, condemnation, and death to the race, while Christ's one act brings righteousness and life to all who receive Him. The parallel holds, but in every comparison the gift is greater than the offense.

Paul says the law came in so that the offense would increase, making sin visible and showing how great it is. But where sin increased, grace super-abounded; the Greek hyperperisseuō means it overflowed beyond it. God's supply of grace does not merely keep pace with sin, it surpasses it, so wherever sin has done its worst, grace does better. The result is that grace now reigns through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ, just as sin had reigned in death.

Reconciliation means that a broken relationship is restored: we who were enemies of God have been brought into friendship with Him through the death of His Son. Justification is a legal verdict in God's courtroom that declares the sinner righteous. Reconciliation is relational, ending the hostility so that the former enemy becomes a child welcomed home. Paul adds that if we were reconciled by Christ's death while enemies, much more we will be saved by His life, and so we rejoice in God.

In Romans 6 Paul argues that grace does not give permission to keep sinning, because the believer has died to sin through union with Christ. Pictured in baptism, the believer was buried with Christ and raised to walk in newness of life; the old man was crucified so we are no longer sin's slaves. Believers must therefore reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God and stop presenting their bodies to sin. Everyone serves some master, and the slave of sin earns death while the slave of God receives eternal life as a gift.

Since Paul has just said that where sin abounded grace abounded much more, someone could reason that sinning more would give grace more chance to shine. Paul raises the question himself and answers with mē genoito, one of the strongest denials in the Greek New Testament: "Certainly not!" or "God forbid!" His reason is that believers have died to sin, so continuing to live in it is a contradiction, like a corpse keeping house with what killed it. Grace does not encourage sin; it breaks sin's hold.

Baptism by immersion pictures two things: going down into the water is burial with Christ into His death, and coming up is resurrection with Him to walk in newness of life. Paul uses this familiar rite to show that believers are truly identified with Christ in His death and resurrection. Baptism does not save or create this union; salvation is in Christ and received by faith. But baptism portrays the union, is an act of obedience, and is a public confession of faith.
Being baptized creates our union with Christ, so the unbaptized are not buried and raised with Him

The old man is the unconverted self, the person under Adam, inclined toward sin by nature and helpless under its rule. Paul says this old self was nailed to the cross with Christ so that the body of sin might be done away with and we would no longer be slaves of sin. It does not mean the believer can no longer be tempted or never sins. It means sin's dominating power has been broken, the old master no longer owns us, and a new person raised by Christ now lives.

"Reckon" translates logizomai, the same bookkeeping word used of righteousness credited to Abraham. To reckon ourselves dead to sin is to count as true what God says is already true because of our union with Christ: we died with Him and rose with Him. It is not pretending or positive thinking but recognizing reality and then acting on it. From that settled identity flow the commands not to let sin reign and to present ourselves to God as alive from the dead.

Paul says that whoever we present ourselves to obey, we are that one's slaves, either of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness. The question is not whether we will serve but whom we will serve. Personal autonomy, the idea that we serve nothing, is a myth, because every human being is enslaved to something. Serving sin steadily destroys us, while serving God steadily shapes us into the likeness of His Son.

Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Wages are earned: sin pays its workers exactly what they have worked for, which is death, spiritual now, physical later, and eternal in the end. Eternal life, however, is not a wage at all but a free gift that cannot be earned. The verse sets out two roads and two destinations, one earned and one given.

A married woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives; if she joins another man while he lives, she is an adulteress, but if he dies she is free to remarry without sin. Paul applies this to the believer and the law. Through the body of Christ, believers have died to the law, so the relationship that bound them to it has ended by death. Now they are free to belong to another, to the risen Christ, and to bear fruit for God.

Believers are released from the law because they died with Christ, so what held them no longer has a claim on them, and they are joined to the risen Christ. This release is not freedom from serving God but a new way of serving. The old way was the oldness of the letter, external rules trying to control unchanged hearts. The new way is the newness of the Spirit, an inner transformation that produces willing obedience from a changed nature, out of love for the One who set us free.

Romans 3-5 shows that believers are declared righteous by faith, and Romans 6 shows that the same union with Christ that justifies also transforms. Because we died and rose with Christ, sin's dominion is broken, so the justified person cannot comfortably keep living in sin. Paul even uses the same word, logizomai: God credited righteousness to us, and now we reckon ourselves dead to sin and alive to God. Sanctification is the daily decision to live out that settled identity, presenting ourselves to God, so grace makes us more serious about holiness, not less.

Paul first defends the law: it is holy, just, and good, and it reveals sin rather than causing it. The real problem is sin, which uses the commandment as an opportunity to stir up more evil desire and so brings death. Then Paul describes the believer's inner war: the new self delights in God's law and wants the good, but indwelling sin in the flesh keeps pulling him into what he hates. This struggle drives him to cry, "O wretched man that I am!" and he immediately thanks God that deliverance comes through Jesus Christ, with full victory at the resurrection.

Paul answers "Is the law sin?" with mē genoito, certainly not. The law is the diagnostician, not the disease: Paul would not have known coveting was sin unless the law had said, "You shall not covet." Like a flashlight in a dark room, the law shows the hazards that were already there without creating them. So Paul concludes the law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good; the problem is the sinful heart the law exposes.

Sin takes opportunity through the commandment and produces all kinds of evil desire. The commandment does not create the impulse, but it gives it a clear target, like telling a child not to touch the hot stove or telling someone not to think of an elephant. Sin uses the very prohibitions meant to restrain it as material for more rebellion. So the law that should lead to life becomes, through sin, the occasion of death, and sin is exposed as exceedingly sinful.

Paul confesses that he does not do the good he wants but does the evil he hates. The problem is not knowing what is right but failing to do it. There are two "I"s in the believer: the new self, regenerated by the Spirit, that wants the good, and the residual sinful nature still living in the body that keeps doing evil. They are not equals, since the new nature is supreme, but the old one is not yet dead, so Paul can say it is no longer he who does it but sin dwelling in him, while still taking responsibility.

A man who truly decides to quit smoking throws away his cigarettes, prays, and is fully convinced the habit is harming him, yet a few hours later he is buying another pack and hating himself for it. He did not want to, he had decided not to, and he did it anyway. That is Paul's experience in Romans 7: the desire to stop and the old habit are both real and live in the same person. It shows that the struggle is not ignorance of what is right but the power of indwelling sin over a sincerely renewed will.

Unbelievers are not wretched over their sin; they are comfortable in it. Only a regenerate heart that delights in God's law feels the painful gap between what it wants to do and what it actually does. So the cry "O wretched man that I am!" is itself evidence that the new nature has taken hold. As the lesson puts it, the dead do not lament their corpses; the living do.

In the ancient world a murderer was sometimes punished by being chained to the corpse of his victim, forced to drag the dead body everywhere until he himself died. Paul uses this image for the indwelling sin still lodged in his mortal body. It feels like a corpse he must drag around, a weight he cannot put down. The old nature is not yet fully dead, but it no longer has the life it once had, and he longs to be freed from it.

Paul immediately answers his own cry: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" The Deliverer is named and the deliverance has already been provided. The complete victory waits for the resurrection, when the body of death will be exchanged for a body of glory, but Christ is at work now, and the assurance of final victory lets the believer keep fighting. Paul still admits that until then, with the mind he serves God's law but with the flesh the law of sin.

Romans 7 honestly describes the real war between the new nature and indwelling sin, and Romans 8 gives the answer to that struggle. Chapter 8 makes the Spirit's power in the battle its theme: there is no condemnation, there is power for victory, and there is glory ahead. The believer who cried "wretched man" in chapter 7 hears in chapter 8 that nothing can separate him from God's love in Christ. Romans 7 is the necessary doorway to the confidence of Romans 8.

Justification is God's instant legal declaration that the believer is righteous, freeing him from sin's penalty. Sanctification is the ongoing process, a daily war, in which the believer, already freed from sin's dominion, fights against the sin still present in his body and grows in holiness. Glorification is the future completion at the resurrection, when the body of death is exchanged for a body of glory and the war ends. In short, justification was instantaneous, sanctification is a war, and glorification is the day that war is over.

Romans 8:1 says there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. The "therefore" looks back to what Christ has done: because He died and rose, because the believer is justified, and because the Spirit now lives in him, no condemnation remains. This is not a partial pardon or a postponed sentence but no condemnation at all, now or ever. The verdict already given in Christ is the final word over the believer's life, which answers the wretched-man cry of chapter 7.

Here "law" (nomos) means a governing principle, like the law of gravity. The law of sin still in the body pulls the believer down, but the law of the Spirit of life in Christ lifts him up. Just as an airplane's aerodynamics overcome gravity without abolishing it, the Spirit's stronger principle overcomes sin's pull. The believer still feels the tug of sin but is empowered to rise above it.

Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on what the flesh desires, and those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on what the Spirit desires. Paul says the carnal mind is death, not merely headed toward it; it is hostile to God, cannot submit to His law, and cannot please Him. The spiritual mind is life and peace. Believers are in the Spirit if God's Spirit dwells in them, and the same Spirit who raised Jesus lives in them, so they live from spiritual life rather than working toward it.

In the Greco-Roman world adoption was not a backup plan but the deliberate choice of an heir, and an adopted son inherited equally with natural sons. So believers have been deliberately chosen, brought into God's family, and given the full rights of heirs. Instead of a spirit of slavery and fear, we receive the Spirit of adoption and cry "Abba, Father," the intimate Aramaic word a small child uses for his daddy. The Spirit testifies with our spirit that we are God's children, and therefore heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ.

First, creation groans: it was subjected to futility by God and waits for its own redemption when God's children are revealed. Second, we believers groan, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, as we wait for the redemption of our bodies. Third, the Spirit Himself groans within us, interceding for us with groanings too deep for words. Together they show that present suffering is real but cannot compare with the glory to come.

Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness, because we often do not know what to pray for as we ought. When grief is too deep, the situation too complex, or the future too uncertain, the Spirit Himself prays for us with groanings too deep for words. The Father, who searches the hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit. Because the Spirit intercedes according to God's will, the prayer always lands.

Romans 8:28 says that all things work together for good to those who love God and are called according to His purpose. It does not say that all things are good; some of the ingredients in a believer's life are bitter, painful, or look like pure loss. What it says is that God blends and weaves them together into something that will in the end be for the believer's good and His glory. The promise is also for those who love God and are called, not a blanket guarantee that everything will turn out pleasant for everyone.

Evelyn Christenson suffered two miscarriages and a stillbirth, but through Romans 8:28 she came to see that her losses were not meaningless; God used them to draw her closer to Him. Roger Irving lost an arm, two infant sons, his savings, his voice, and an eye, yet believed God had a worthwhile purpose for his life. His losses became turning points: sales, Scouting with hundreds of boys, a new valuing of his wife and of God over money, and teaching esophageal speech to others. Neither claimed God caused the tragedies, but both show God turning suffering into good, and his wife learned from Christ's suffering on the cross to endure in her small way.

In Romans 8:29-30 Paul lists five links: those God foreknew He predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son; those He predestined He called; those He called He justified; and those He justified He glorified. Every link is forged by God Himself, not by us. From God's standpoint each is already accomplished, which is why Paul even speaks of glorification in the past tense. The chain shows how certain the believer's final salvation is.

After building his case, Paul asks, "If God is for us, who can be against us?" and argues from greater to lesser: if God did not spare His own Son, He will surely give us all things with Him. No one can bring a charge, because God justifies, and no one can condemn, because Christ died, rose, and intercedes for us. In tribulation, persecution, famine, and sword we are more than conquerors, not after escaping them but in them. Paul then lists every category of created reality, death, life, angels, powers, present, future, height, depth, anything else, and declares that none can separate us from God's love in Christ, which answers the wretched-man cry with unbreakable certainty.
God is against us for our sin and will not spare us from His charge

Right after the triumph of Romans 8, Paul writes with great sorrow and continual grief for his fellow Jews, who have largely rejected their Messiah. He says he could even wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ if that would save his kinsmen, a wish he knows cannot be granted but that shows how deeply he carries them. He lists Israel's privileges: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the temple service, the promises, the patriarchs, and Christ Himself according to the flesh. No nation was more favored, which makes their unbelief all the more painful to him.

Paul says God's word has not failed, because not everyone descended from Israel is truly Israel. There has always been an ethnic Israel, Abraham's physical descendants, and a true Israel within it, those who share Abraham's faith as well as his bloodline. God's promises were never made to everyone with the right ancestry but to those He chose as heirs of the promise. This matters because it explains how God remains faithful even though much of ethnic Israel rejected the Messiah.

Abraham had two biological sons, but the promise went through Isaac, not Ishmael. Isaac had twin sons, and before they were born or had done anything good or bad, God said the older would serve the younger, choosing Jacob over Esau. These examples show that even within the chosen family the promise moved forward by God's sovereign election. It was not based on physical descent, birth order, or merit.

When someone objects that God is unjust to choose some and not others, Paul asks who we are to talk back to God. A potter has the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, and the clay cannot demand an explanation. The image teaches that mercy is God's prerogative and salvation is not owed to anyone; He has mercy on whom He will. Yet His purpose is gracious: He has called vessels of mercy prepared for glory from both Jews and Gentiles.

Israel pursued righteousness, but as if it could be gained by works of the law rather than by faith. So they stumbled over the stumbling stone, which is Christ, while Gentiles who were not even seeking righteousness obtained it by faith. Paul says Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, meaning both its goal and its completion. Israel was responsible for refusing the righteousness God offered in Christ, even though God is sovereign.

Romans 10:9-13 says that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved, because whoever calls on the name of the Lord, Jew or Gentile, will be saved. The righteousness Israel sought through the law is near and offered to anyone who believes. Then Paul asks how people can call on someone they have not believed, believe in someone they have not heard of, hear without a preacher, or preach unless they are sent. That is the Great Commission inside the letter: because salvation comes by hearing and believing, preachers must be sent, and their feet are beautiful.

Paul pictures God's people as one cultivated olive tree rooted in the promise to Abraham, not two separate trees for Israel and the church. Some natural branches, unbelieving Jews, were broken off because of unbelief, and wild branches, Gentile believers, were grafted in by faith. Natural branches can be grafted back in when they believe. So believing Jews and Gentiles share the same root and nourishment; Gentiles must not boast, because the root supports them, and branches stay or are removed according to faith, not ethnicity.

Within the one-olive-tree picture, the most natural reading is that "all Israel" means the full people of God, Jewish and Gentile believers together, gathered across the whole of redemptive history. Many faithful interpreters also expect a large future turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, but as natural branches grafted back into the same tree, not as a separate program. On either reading, all Israel is saved in Christ, by faith, as part of the one people of God. There is no second covenant and no separate destiny for ethnic Israel apart from the church.

It means God never takes back what He has given or the call He has made; He does not abandon what He has begun. Israel's hardening was therefore never a permanent rejection. It opened the door for the Gentiles and was meant to provoke Israel to jealousy and faith, while Gentile salvation is meant to draw Jewish hearts back to the Messiah. God has bound all, Jews and Gentiles, over to disobedience so that He might have mercy on all.

After three chapters on election, Israel's unbelief, and the salvation of the Gentiles, Paul cannot fit God's wisdom into a neat system. God turns Israel's unbelief into salvation for the Gentiles and then uses the Gentiles' salvation to provoke Israel to faith; His sovereign mercy and human responsibility are beyond our full understanding. So Paul breaks into praise: "Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" No one has counseled God or given Him something first, because all things are of Him, through Him, and to Him. Worship is the only honest response to a mercy that great.

With "therefore," Paul moves from eleven chapters of doctrine to practical living. He does not command but beseeches, appealing to the mercies of God already shown, because mercy received is the strongest motive for Christian living. In place of the Old Testament's dead animal, he asks believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, their reasonable service. The whole life is surrendered daily, and since a living sacrifice can crawl off the altar, the offering must be renewed every morning.

To be conformed is to be squeezed from the outside into the world's mold. To be transformed, from the Greek metamorphoō, is to be changed from the inside out by the renewing of the mind. A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by being pressed into a butterfly-shaped mold but by an inner change, and Christian growth works the same way. Both verbs are present tense, so the Christian life is a daily contest between the world's pressure and the Spirit's ongoing transformation.

Paul warns believers not to think too highly of themselves but to use sober judgment, since each has a measure of faith but no one has every gift. Like a body with many members and different functions, we are one body in Christ and members of one another. He lists gifts such as prophecy, serving, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, and showing mercy, and tells each to use his gift diligently. The key principle is that gifts are tools to build the body with, not toys to play with or weapons to fight with, so healthy church life is complementarity, each member serving in his own role.

Paul tells believers not to repay evil for evil but, as far as it depends on them, to live at peace with everyone, admitting that some conflicts cannot be ended by one side. They must not take revenge but leave room for God's wrath, because vengeance belongs to the Lord. Instead they should feed a hungry enemy and give him a drink, which heaps coals of fire on his head. In the Old Testament coals of fire are a picture of God's judgment, so the point is that the believer can return good for evil, trusting God with the final reckoning, and overcome evil with good.

Paul says every person should be subject to the governing authorities, because all authority comes from God and existing authorities are appointed by Him to restrain evil, reward good, and bear the sword for justice. First distinction: "be subject" is not identical to "obey"; submission includes respect and a willingness to accept the consequences when conscience requires disobedience, as when the apostles said, "We ought to obey God rather than men." Second distinction: church and state have different spheres and should not be merged. Practically, believers pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor to whom they are due.

Paul says to owe no one anything except to love one another. Christians pay their bills and taxes, but the debt of love can never be paid off; it is always outstanding. The commandments against adultery, murder, stealing, false witness, and coveting are all summed up in "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." Because love does no wrong to a neighbor, love fulfills the law and already honors everything the law was protecting.

Paul says it is high time to wake from sleep, because our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed; the night is almost over and the day is at hand. So believers must put off the works of darkness, like revelry, drunkenness, immorality, strife, and envy, and put on the armor of light. Above all they must put on the Lord Jesus Christ and make no provision for the flesh. This repeats 12:1-2: the body offered, the mind renewed, and Christ worn like clothing each morning.

The weak in faith are believers whose conscience requires more restraint, for example abstaining from certain foods or honoring special days, not because their faith is defective but because their conscience has not yet rested in the full liberty Christ won. The strong are those whose conscience allows more freedom. Paul says both are accepted by the Lord, so the strong must not despise the weak and the weak must not judge the strong. Each is the Lord's servant, stands or falls before his own Master, and will give account to God for himself.

Romans 14:17 says the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Christianity is not finally about menus or calendars. So disagreements over food or special days should not divide believers or become tests of fellowship. Instead we should pursue what makes for peace and builds one another up, holding to Christ and to each other in love rather than demanding identical opinions.

The principle means that a Christian who acts against his own conscience sins, even if the act itself is lawful, because he is not acting in faith. It cuts one way against the strong: they must not push the weak into doing things their conscience cannot accept, and they should even give up eating meat or drinking wine if it makes a brother stumble, since all things are lawful but not all are helpful.
